speechtext: Bill (No. 122) further to amend the General Inspection Act.-Hon. Mr. Bernier.
The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE (Hon. M. E. Bernier) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 123) to amend the Manitoba Grain Act, 1900.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bernier) be good enough to explain the purport of the Bill ?

The changes are very few. The first clause is to empower the Governor General in Council either to reduce or increase the scale of fees. The second change is to provide for the deposit to the credit of the Receiver General of all fees collected, instead of depositing them to the credit of what is called the Manitoba Inspection Fund. The inspectors and deputy inspectors are either paid by fees or by commission out of the treasury. The next clause is to the same effect, providing for the money collected from the inspectors and sub-inspectors being placed in the Receiver General's hands. The last amendment is to the same effect.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Bill (No. 11S) to amend the Yukon Territory Act and to make further provision for the administration of justice in the said territory-the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Clifford Sifton) read iilie second time, and considered in committee.

I very much doubt the advisability of permitting these police magistrates to practise their profession. I know that in cities in the eastern portion of the Dominion where these magistrates are given a very considerable jurisdiction, they are not permitted to practise, and I think that the reasons which hold good in the east would have even greater application in the Yukon district. Would the hon. minister state the reasons because of which he thinks it desirable that these gentlemen shall be given permission to practise their profession while occupying these judicial positions.

The great difficulty that arises in connection with the appointment of an officer of sufficiently good standing as a professional man to occupy these positions would be that we would have to pay him in all probability as high a salary

as we pay to a judge, if we debarred him from practising liis profession. The idea of the Minister of Justice was that we would be able to secure, for possibly $1,500 a year, the services of competent professional men to act as police magistrates if they would be able to earn additional remuneration by practising their profession outside. From the government standpoint it is purely a question of not being compelled to pay a salary which would be considered high, as we would have to put the police magistrate on the same footing as other officials by paying him living allowance and salary, which would be pretty expensive altogether. I recognize that the point raised by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) is open to debate. I understand that in the other House the question was discussed for some time, and it was only after considerable discussion that this section was agreed to. If the hon. the leader of the opposition^ presses the point very strongly I will be content to reserve the clause and confer with the Minister of Justice again.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext: I would be glad if the hon. gentleman would take that course. I require some time to consider the matter myself. There are worse things than paying salaries of $4,000 or $5,000 a year to these men. It would be infinitely better to do that than that we should have any scandal about the administration of justice in the Yukon.
I agree.

In my own province in cases where these gentlemen have pretty large jurisdiction, they are not allowed to practice, and that course has been found to be the best on the whole. It might occur that money saved in the way indicated in the Bill would not be money saved in the best interests of the country.

Section 6 provides that the Governor in Council can give a police magistrate civil jurisdiction, and in the exception clause there is nothing to prevent his partner practising before him in these cases as the exception apparently only refers to criminal cases.

The wording of the section, I think, is sufficient to prevent that. It says :
No such police magistrate and no partner or clerk of any such police magistrate shall act as agent or solicitor or counsel in any case, matter or proceeding of a criminal nature, or in any case tried before such police magistrate.
The words * or in any case,' would include civil matters.
That may be.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: That would apply only to a case which is tried or investigated, but it does not seem to apply to a case which is instituted. The language of the section might be broadened a little in that respect.
It is possible that the wording of the section might be better. I will note the point.

I have very strong objections to allowing a judge or a quasi judge to practise his profession. The effect is often to send people to the office of the justice of the peace or his partner in cases which might properly come before the court, but which, when they went there, never did come before it. I think the best course is to pay a good officer to be a police magistrate, and not let him touch law in any other way. If he is a good man, I am sure that is the only way of keeping him free from suspicion ; and if he is not a good man, we do not want him.
Surely the hon. gentleman would not advocate prohibiting a police magistrate from practising in the Court of Chancery ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Not if he has no civil jurisdiction; but if he has, the same reason applies, and in a stronger degree; because he might be able to arrange matters as another lawyer could not. I see no reason to prevent a police magistrate practising in the civil courts if he has no civil jurisdiction; but if he has civil jurisdiction, then civil cases should not be entertained by him or his partner. In the province of Ontario, in the early days of masters in chancery in the country, masters and their partners were allowed to practise and also to occupy the position of master in chancery; but that was eventually changed, owing to troubles and suspicions that arose.

I remember very well the stipendiary magistrates in my native town having both criminal jurisdiction and also civil jurisdiction up to small amounts. That was the case for thirty years at least, and I do not remember a case in which their right to practise in the superior courts was ever questioned.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Did their civil jurisdiction extend to the collection of debts ?
Small debts up to $150.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
The magistrates under the Bill have jurisdiction over large amounts-up to $500 in some cases and in

others up to $1,000. It seems an extensive jurisdiction.

The jurisdiction is more extensive in civil matters than the jurisdiction of the county court judges of the province of Nova Scotia, who, I think, would be surprised if they were allowed to practise in the superior courts.

I wish to add my word to the view that magistrates should not be allowed to practise. If you allow a magistrate possessing this extensive jurisdiction to practise in the courts, I venture to say that within six months you will have a lot of complaints on your hands. I say, give him a good salary, and debar him from practising, especially in that country where he would not probably be required to act according to the rules of etiquette to the same extent that he would in the older provinces.
On section 4,

The experience demanded by this section does not appear to be very great. I suppose the hon. gentleman has considered that carefully, and has the sanction of the Minister of Justice for this provision.

I may say that it embodies the view of the Minister of Justice after careful consideration. I cannot see that a requirement that a man would be a barrister of five years' standing would be much more protection to the public than a requirement that he should be one of three years' standing.

It may be that it is sometimes best to catch them young.
On section 5,
Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to explain the exact effect of the words which provide that ' his jurisdiction under the said part shall be absolute without the consent of the person charged.'

I will explain that later.
On section 6,
Might I ask the minister what other judges are up there ?
There are two judges of the territorial court.

I cannotj form any opinion as to how much work they have to do, but it does seem to me an extraordinary departure from the usual practice followed in the older provinces to give a police magistrate control over such an important amount of judicial or civil work. This certainly would require much higher qualifications than is exacted by this section. The police magistrate need only have read a small amount of law and have only practised as advocate or solicitor three years, and in that experience the majority of gentlemen likely to be up there would have acquired but little knowledge.

The chief difficulty is that the judges are very much overworked and pressure has been brought on the government to appoint additional judges. As is the case in all new districts, a large amount of litigation has accumulated, which in all probability will be pretty well thinned out in a year or two. and the government have hesitated about, increasing the number of judges, because once the number is increased it is practically impossible to reduce it. Then, except in summer there is practically no communication between White Horse and Dawson City. Dux'ing the long winter the only communication is over the ice, and the expense of sending a judge and the necessary paraphernalia from Dawson to White Horse, besides the exposure to the weather, presents a great obstacle to holding a circuit court. The idea of the Minister of Justice was to appoint a police magistrate at White Horse who would have this jurisdiction, but the police magistrate at Dawson at least after the first short while, would only have criminal jurisdiction and civil jurisdiction in trifling cases.

I am in receipt of a letter from one of the leading practitioners in Dawson who informs me that since Christmas the court has been sitting every day and sometimes at night, and that there is still a large amount of business which the judges have not been able to touch. The work in a new country is much greater than it is here, and I am satisfied that a necessity exists for these appointments, and also for the jurisdiction given these magistrates. The Superior Court has to try a great many cases relating to mining. There is one case which took the time of the court every day of the week for a fortnight, relating to a mining claim in which a couple of hundred thousand dollars were Involved, and such eases require very patient and long hearing, so that it would be impossible for the two judges to overtake all the small cases that come before them.
On section 9,
It seems to me the right of appeal is somewhat limited by this section.

I
observe that too. and I will reserve that section.

It wouid be just as well to do so, because there might be a

claim amounting to upwards of $500 as to which there would be no appeal.

Let that stand. I may say that after the Bill was introduced in the Senate the Surveyor General called my attention to the fact that the description of the Yukon territory had necessarily been somewhat vague from a scientific standpoint when the Act was originally passed, and he advised me that it would be well to have a new description made in accordance with the information which the Surveyor General's branch has since acquired in regard to the territory, and to substitute it for the description in the original Act. I have, therefore, had an amendment prepared for the purpose of amending the description. The boundary line will not be substantially altered except in one respect. The territory will be a little enlarged, and a portion of the valley of the Peel river, which, under the old description, has belonged to the North-west Territories, is now brought into the Yukon Territory, and properly, I think, because it will be nearer the seat of government at Dawson and more conveniently governed than from Regina. I therefore propose the following amendment :
That section 2 of the Yukon Territory Act, chap. 6, of the Statutes of 189S, is hereby repealed, and the following section Is substituted therefor :
2. The territory described in the schedule of this Act is hereby constituted and declared to be a separate territory under the name of the Yukon territory, and the same shall no longer form part of the North-west Territories.
In section 14 follows the technical description of the territory in accordance with the plaep which I have handed to my hon. friend.
This" is for all purposes, and not solely for judicial purposes.
For all purposes.

Other things being equal, it would be better to deal with the subject by a separate Act, I should suppose. It seems to me a little incongruous to introduce it into an Act appointing a police magistrate.

I do not know whether I made myself clear. In the original Yukon Territory Act is contained a description of the territory, and by that Act the territory is described as withdrawn from the North-west Territories and formed into a separate territory. The description from a scientific standpoint is not so saticfactory as we could wish. Further Information has been acquired by recent explorations that have taken place which re-

quire a different description. But it makes no difference in the territory except as to a small portion of the Feel river valley. It will be more easily administered from Dawson City than it would be by the territorial government at Regina. I may say that persons have gone lately into the territory of the head waters of the Peel river, and have made applications to the commissioner's office in Dawson City for the purpose of having their mining claims recorded, and it is not likely, according to the original description, that the territory is in the Yukon. There is a doubt in the description as to the actual location of the boundary line, and we now include the head waters of the Peel river and bring it into the Yukon
territory-

The hon. gentleman must see that the description of the eastern boundary is almost impossible to lay out upon the ground. The southern boundary, of course, is a parallel of latitude, except the part that is near the coast. The question is this : If a crime is committed where it is impossible to fix the eastern boundary, is there equal jurisdiction in the courts of the North-west Territories and of the Yukon district for the trial of such a case ?

I cannot answer that question. I think there is a general Act under which either of the criminal courts would have jurisdiction. The object in fixing this line, is as far as possible, to follow the watershed as the natural boundary, the territory on the north-west side of the water-shed belonging to the Yukon and on the east side to the Northwest Territories.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I think the objection raised by my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden) is a proper one, when he says that it is obvious that, as this refers to another matter than that covered by the other part of the Bill, it should form a separate Act by itself. You amend the Yukon Territory Act by a clause inserted in a Bill affecting the judicial courts of the territory. If this affected the territory only in relation to judicial matters, it would be all right, but it affects it in every way, and should be dealt with separately. There is no objection to the amendment itself, but it should be a separate Bill, as it has nothing to do with the other part of the Act.

My hon. friend (Mr. LaRiviSre) will see that the Yukon Territory Act dealt writh the question of description, and also with the question of judicial arrangement ; and, this Bill being brought in to amend that Act, it is certainly germane to the subject to amend any portion of the Yukon Territory Act. I do not think it would add to the convenience of reference, which is the only question

involved in the hon. gentleman's suggestion, to make one more Act than seems necessary. It seems to me that it would be best to have amendments to the Yukon Territory Act included in one measure, so that if a man is, looking for amendments and finds this Act, he knows that he has them all before him.
Is there any international arrangement with the United States authorities as to the boundary at that part of the line where you depart from the line of latitude near the coast ?

As to the portion of the territory which lies contiguous to Alaska, there is a provisional boundary line agreed to between the two governments, and that line, wherever necessary, has been laid down upon the ground by commissioners appointed by the parties. Our commissioner and the commissioner of the United States went up last season and laid out the boundary line at the only place practically necessary, that is, across the Dalton trail to Pyramid Harbour. Under the terms of the provisional arrangement, the summit of the White Pass, the pass through which the railway runs, and the summit of the Chilkoot Pass, which was also used oy travellers before the railway was opened, are considered to be the provisional boundary line. They are fixed by agreement. So, we have at all the passes where travel is possible, a fixed provisional boundary line, and there can be no difficulty about administration.
Does the description follow that line ? My object in making these remarks is

I would ask to be allowed to interrupt my hon. friend. I did not touch upon one point which, perhaps, would have made the matter clearer. The part of the Canadian territory which comes into immediate contact with Alaska at the point mentioned is in British Columbia. The boundary line of the Yukon territory is further north, so that a question does not arise as between Alaska and the Yukon, but between Alaska and British Columbia. That is to say, if you start north from Skagway, you go through the White Pass to the summit, at which point the provisional boundary line is fixed between Canada and the United States. But, when you cross the White Pass, you are in British Columbia, and you have to go half way over Lake Bennett before you strike the OOtli parallel of latitude and reach the Yukon territory.
Then, I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the boundary we are fixing now is not the boundary between the Yukon territory and any part of the United States ?

It is not quite so wide as that. When you get across past the place which is disputed, over to the eastern boundary of Alaska properly' speaking, you come in contact with the eastern boundary of Alaska, following the 60th parallel of latitude. But, that is not where the question in dispute arises. I will read the description as prepared by the Surveyor General :
The Yukon territory shall be bounded as follows :-
On the south by the province of British Columbia and the United States territory of Alaska;

So, you do not touch the American boundary at any place where there is a dispute as to boundaries

Tbe hon. gentleman's description covers tbe objection I might otherwise have made. At the southerly point he makes the boundary the United States territory of Alaska. I should have objected to laying down a line which might give the solemn affirmation of an Act of parliament to a fixed point, and might so interfere with negotiations afterwards. I see that he has carefully avoided that.

Amendment agreed to.
Progress reported.

Bill (No. 115) to amend the General Inspection Act-The Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. AI. E. Bernier) read the second time, and considered in committee.
On section 1,

I think the hon. gentleman stated when introducing this

Bill that the grades have been submitted to him by the Winnipeg Board of Trade.
Yes.
Does the board of trade represent the wishes of the province in respect to this ?

I suppose so. There is no change in the grade of No. 1 Manitoba hard wheat. The grade of No. 2 Manitoba hard wheat is incorporated with No. 1 Manitoba northern wheat. There is no change in No. 1 Manitoba northern. No. 2 Manitoba northern is unchanged except that the quantity of red fife wheat necessary to the grade is changed from 50 to 45 lbs. The old law is changed to provide that scoured wheat shall not grade higher than No. 3 northern. A new grade of No. 3 Manitoba northern is added to the list, and the grade of No. 2 Manitoba hard and No. 1 Manitoba northern have been consolidated under the name of No. 1 Manitoba northern. These changes are made on the recommendation of the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Exchange and the Standard Board with the result of bringing the grades more within the composition of those of Minnesota and Dakota.

Would the hon. minister briefly state whether the changes will have the effect of raising the standard or lowering it ? I see by the papers that Manitoba wheat has not the sale it used to have or the reputation in the old country where it used to be purchased chiefly on account of its grade. Is that caused by a lax inspection or by the alteration of the grades ?
I think the main feature of the Bill is rather to assimilate the grade of wheat in Manitoba with those of Dakota and Minnesota.

I think I understand my hon. friend's point as to the difficulty that has arisen. It was taken under review by the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Bernier) who appointed a commission for the purpose of looking into the matter and of investigating it. I am bound to say that I have not had an opportunity of looking at the report of the commission, but, I have no dqubt at all that the difficulty was of two kinds, first, on account of the undue variations in the grade which is a question that we have been fighting about in Manitoba for years, too great flexibility in the changing of the grade, and second, some carelessness in the inspection at the port of Montreal. By the appointment of this commission of experienced men, the chairman of which was Mr. David Horn, the inspector at Winnipeg, I believe a very capable man, so considered by grain men, they have ar-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
rived at a plan which will enable the western wheat to be graded separately, and there can be then no excuse for mixing it with other grades and the reputation of that wheat will be preserved.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

maintopic: CULLING OF LUMBER AND INSPECTION OF STAPLES.
speechtext: What is the meaning of this Bill ?

House again in Committee of Supply. Kamloops public building, $11,600.

['I do not dare to make any promise in the absence of the chairman, but I hope we will be able to meet on Friday. The reason for postponing the meeting on Wednesday is one which is common to both sides and it is a well understood rule that in such a case the committee meetings are cancelled. I hope there shall be a meeting on Friday morning, but without consulting the chairman, I do not care to make a more definite statement.']
Will the hon. gentleman explain ?

This is to complete the work, which is now under contract. The money was voted last year.
Nelson public building, $15,000.

I am sorry to say that this will not be sufficient to complete the work. $20,000 was voted last year, and we are now asking $15,000 for the work which will be done this year. It will require $25,000 more to complete the work. I am very sorry to say that work is more expensive in British Columbia than in any other part of Canada. Wages are 50 or 75 per cent higher there.
Is the cost of living higher ?

Yes, I quite grant that. For instance, while I pay men $22 or $25 a month for dredging on the St. Lawrence, I have to pay them $50 a month in British Columbia; and everything else is very much higher there.
You do not pay the Frenchmen whom you take there from Quebec a higher price, do you ?

I do not take men from Quebec; but we pay men there $50 a month. I do not complain. I simply state the facts in order to explain to the House that if the works cost more in British Columbia, it is to a large extent due to higher wages and the greater cost of living.
Do I understand the minister to say that he has men working for $22 a month ?
Yes, $22 and board. I pay $50 and board in British Columbia.
What is the amount of the contract for that building ?

$50,000. The site cost $11,000.
New Westminster public building, $17,000.
This will pay the balance of the cost. My hon. friends know that the public building there was destroyed by fire, and we had to rebuild it.
What is the name of the contractor for this building ?
Messrs. Bourque & Desrivieres.
Do -they belong to British Columbia ?
No. We asked for tenders all over the Dominion.
I suppose somebody from Quebec got the contract ?
Somebody from Quebec who was the lowest tenderer got it. Does the hon. gentleman object to a man from Quebec getting a contract when he is the lowest tenderer ?
I was simply asking the question. The hon. gentleman need not lose his temper.
But the hon. gentleman asked it in such a way as to imply that he thought it was wrong to give a contract to a Quebec firm even if it was the lowest.

If the hon. gentleman wants to know, I do think it wrong. I think that for buildings put up in British Columbia, British Columbia contractors and labourers should have a little better chance than contractors in the east. Everybody knows that eastern contractors tender for work at too low a price, and afterwards they manage with the department by hook or by crook to get a lot of extras allowed, which will bring up the price.

I am in the hands of the House and the country. The money voted by this House for these works is the money of the country-the money of Quebec, Ontario, and the maritime provinces more than of British Columbia.
No.

Yes. The larger provinces supply more than the smaller provinces. I do not complain of that; but if the hon. gentleman, who is an ex-minister of the Crown, lays down the principle that even the lowest tenderer must not get the contract, I want to know it now, and not later on. I am very glad the hon. gentleman has laid down that sound principle. If the men of the east should not get a contract in the west, then the system is no good.

Oh, yes, it is. The hon. gentleman says the money is more eastern money than British Columbia money. Let me tell him that British Columbia has paid more into the Dominion treasury than she ever got out of it. Since British Columbia went into confederation, she has paid over $42,000,000 into the Dominion treasury, and has received back only a little over $29,000,000; so that we still have a large balance in the Dominion treasury to our credit. With regard to these contracts, the hon. gentleman notices that everything is higher in

British Columljia, wages and materials of all kinds, and the people expect larger profits. I contend that British Columbia contractors and labourers, who have to live at a higher rate than eastern men, should be given a preference in any contracts that are let there. The eastern men put in a tender at a price at which they think they can do the work in the east, with a little addition for higher labour, and if they make a little profit, they come east with it and are satisfied; whereas the British Columbia man makes a profit and spends it in the country; and I contend that we in the west have a perfect right to have a little privilege given to our own contractors, so that the money will be kept in the province.

If my hon. friend looks at the next item, Rossland public building, he will find that that is being built by a man from Vancouver. My hon. friend, I am sure, is not serious in saying that when a contractor from any province is lower than the men from his own province, we must pass him over. He will not say it again.
Yes, I will.
If the hon. gentleman says so, he will be alone in the House. Everything being equal, and as the hon. gentleman agrees to that, I have nothing more to say.
What was the amount of the original contract ?
Were there several tenderers ?
Six or seven.
Was there a great difference between the tenderers ?
I cannot say off-hand, but will bring the figures down.
Will this finish the building ?
Yes. $65,000 is the total cost.
This is considerably beyond the amount of the contract, which was $55,000.
The contract is for the bare building. This covers besides the furniture and the heating system, and so on.
Are these latter in the same hands ?

No.
Rossland public building, $20,000.

The building will cost altogether $75,000, Mr. PRIOR.
including heating and furnishing. The contract for the bare building is $45,000.
Vancouver drill hall, $19,000.
The newspapers said that a part had tumbled down on account of defective workmanship. What was the matter ?
A part fell down, but, of course, the contractor is bound to finish the work in proper order, and is responsible for what happened.
Who are the contractors, and what was the amount of the contract ?
Viau and Lachance are the contractors- two men from the east again, and they were again the lowest tenderers. The amount of the contract is $65,000.
Does that include the fitting up, or merely the shell of the building ?
Only the bare building.
If a part of the building tumbled down, can these contractors be said to have done good work ?
Eastern men are exposed to accidents the same as western men. I would be very much surprised if western men never met with accidents, though, of course, they are the better men.

I asked the hon. gentleman if he could give any reason for the building tumbling down. When a building of that kind falls down, the accident must be due to bad material or workmanship, or an earthquake, or something of that kind.

I have a report from Mr. Anderson, clerk of the works, and a very able man, who says that the building is first-class in design, and the workmanship and material first-class, but the contractor was too anxious to go ahead, and instead of stopping the work during the wet weather he decided to go on, and the accident consequently happened, for which he is responsible.
Then it was owing to the wet getting into the walls and softening the mortar that the walls gave way.
The report is to that effect.
What is the total cost ?
$96,000, including the fitting up. There is an armoury which has to be finished inside, and heating apparatus, and the electric light, and fencing and sidewalks.
Are all these extras to be given to the same contractor ?
Not necessarily.
They will be given a chance to do the work ?
I do not see why not.
The hon. gentleman gave them a contract for $05,000 for the bare walls, and then gives them a chance to tender for the other work.
They will not be excluded from tendering any more than other contractors.
Will the lowest tender be accepted ?
Certainly.	.
With the permission of the committee, I would again draw attention to the absolute necessity there exists for additional accommodation at the drill hall in Toronto.
Oh, oh.

I will take my seat if the hon. gentleman desires to make remarks on the subject of the Vancouver drill hall, and after he has finished I will try to say what I have to say about the Toronto drill hall. I have offered no objection to an appropriation to complete the drill hall in Vancouver, and I hope to have his support in asking an appropriation to complete the hall in Toronto. And I will try to give reasons why this work should be done. I see the hon. Minister of Militia (Hon. Mr. Borden) in his place, and that is why I ask permission to call the attention of the committee to a matter that has transpired within the last few weeks showing the absolute necessity that exists for additional accommodation. Now, the first letter I shall read to the committee is one from the officer commanding military district No. 2, Col. W. D. Otter :
Stanley Barracks,
Toronto, 22nd March, 1901.
Sir,-I have the honour to make application on behalf of a portion of the local militia force for the temporary use of the [DOT] Arcade,' St. Andrew's market, for the purpose of storing guns, wagons and harness.
With the present strength of the city corps, it is impossible, to find enough accommodation in the armouries, and pending the provision of such, I am compelled to appeal to the municipal authorities, as no place adapted for the purpose in view can be obtained.
I sincerely trust your committee will see its way to recommending my application to the council, and that a favourable answer may be granted.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
W. D. OTTER, Col., Comd'g M. D. No. 2.
The Chairman of the Property Committee,
.	City Hall, Toronto.
This matter was referred by the property committee to the city commissioner ; and this is the report made by the city commissioner upon the application :
(Copy.)
April 10th, 1901.
Chairman and Members,
Property Committee.
Gentlemen,-Your committee have forwarded to me for report the inclosed application of Colonel Otter for the use of the Arcade in St. Andrew's market for the purpose of storing guns, wagons and harness, temporarily, for the local militia force. I beg to report that I have conferred with Mr. Hughes, caretaker of the market, who informs me that there are no shops or Stalls occupied in the building that are entered by way of the Arcade, that the only use made of the Arcade is by persons walking down from the north to the south, but that very few persons are in the habit of going through the Arcade at all, inasmuch as there is no sidewalk across the market square connecting with Adelaide street, therefore, so far as the use of the Arcade is concerned, it is of no value to the public at large, and I fail to see any objection to the temporary compliance with Colonel Otter's request.
Respectfully submitted,

City Commissioner.
The committee reported to the council as follows :
Temporary Use of Arcade in St. Andrew's Market for Storing Guns, &c.
Application has been made to your committee by Col. Otter, commanding M. D. No. 2, on behalf of the local militia force, for the temporary use of the Arcade in St. Andrew's market for the purpose of storing guns, wagons and harness. In his communication, Col. Otter states that with the present strength of the city corps it is impossible to find enough accommodation in the armouries, and pending the provision of such he is compelled to appeal to the municipal authorities, as no place adapted for the purpose in view can be obtained.
The application was referred to the City Commissioner, who has reported thereon as follows : I have read that report.
The committee then recommended as follows
Your committee, after due consideration, beg to recommend that the temporary use of the Arcade in the St. Andrew's market be granted to the local militia force for the purpose indicated, the council reserving the right to terminate this arrangement upon giving one month's notice to Col. Otter, or to such officer as may .be authorized to carry out the duties now performed by him.
I think I am safe in saying that this correspondence discloses a condition of things respecting the accommodation provided for the militia forces of Toronto that is not at all satisfactory, or, indeed, creditable. Appeals have been made time and again, both to the Department of Militia and Department of Public Works asking that the additional accommodation required be furnished. And, if the committee will pardon me for referring to the remarks made by the Minister of Public Works when the question

was last before the House, of providing this additional accommodation, I will quote what he said-especially as the hon. Minister of Militia, his colleague, is now in his seat. Speaking on the 2nd of April, the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) said :
Matters of this kind belong to the Department of Militia and Defence. I am only a builder. If the Department of Militia and Defence asks me to erect an armoury in Toronto, I shall do so with the greatest of pleasure.
I submit to the Minister of Militia and to the Minister of Public Works, that urgency is required in the matter of completing the Toronto drill shed. The delay which has taken place has been an unreasonable delay, and, in view of the presentation of the case to the municipal committee by the officer commanding district No. 2, Col. Otter, who knows the wants and requirements of the militia force of the city, and who knows the accommodation at the drill shed, no stronger case could possibly be made out for immediate action. The hon. minister said that the time to make application was when the supplementary estimates were brought down. X think it is better, with all respect to the Minister of Public Works, to renew this application before the supplementary estimates are brought down. So that, the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Public Works, being seized of the facts contained in the correspondence, may be induced to ask their colleagues to put an appropriation in the estimates to complete the shed. We in the city of Toronto, like the people of other places, are proud of the militia force we have. The men who compose these corps keep them up at considerable loss of time to themselves, and even at considerable expense ; and we think it not unreasonable, considering the sacrifices they make to maintain the force in the splendid state of efficiency in which it now is, that accommodation should be supplied, and arms and accoutrements placed in a safe and convenient place, rather than in a building borrowed temporarily from the municipality for the purpose. St. Andrew's market, for which Col. Otter has applied, is a long distance from the drill shed. It is not as safe a place to store arms and supplies as in the drill shed. It will be a matter of inconvenience to the men to have part of the stores and arms and supplies in one building and another part in another building. And I appeal, not piteously, but straightforwardly, to both the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Militia, that there shall be no longer delay in providing the means to make an addition to the drill shed that will give the accommodation for the militia of Toronto which is so urgently required.
I must say that my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) displays a great deal of energy and zeal on

behalf of the city of Toronto. It is his right to do so, and I may add that it is his duty to do so. I cannot blame him in either case- very far from it. On the other hand, he must not forget that there are many, many calls made upon us from all parts of the country. The great military spirit which has been developed has brought out demands from all quarters. We cannot comply with them all at the same time. That would be out of the question. In such a case, as I said in a former debate, I am a builder. If my colleagues impose upon me the agreeable duty of building an armoury in Toronto or building armouries elsewhere, I will do my level best to give my friends fine buildings. If the money is voted, I will put up the buildings all right. But, again, I must call my hon. friend's attention to the many demands that are made upon us. If we were to comply with them all, I am sure we would be scarified by our hon. friends opposite ; they would point to the large increase in the public expenditure we were making. I do not say that to blame my hon. friend for making these efforts, but only to induce him to have a little patience. There are other parts of the country where people are just as anxious as my hon. friend to have armouries and public buildings. We cannot meet all these demands. But, when the supplementary estimates come down, my hon. friend will see whether his eloquent appeal has had any effect on the Treasury benches.

I desire to put in a word in favour of an armoury for the county I have the honour to represent. We have no armoury at all, while Toronto has a very excellent armoury. It is true they have nearly five corps, and we have one. I would respectfully call the attention of the minister to the fact that the county of Victoria is very anxious to have an armoury, and I trust the hon. gentleman will make a note of it when he is preparing his supplementary estimates.

As armouries seem to be up for discussion, and as I was not present when the St. Thomas item went through, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if it is the policy of the department not to allow Conservatives to have anything to do with the erection of armouries ?

It is certainly not our policy. In the case of the St. Thomas armoury the contract was given after public tender to the lowest tenderer. I do not know whether the contractor is a Conservative or a Liberal, I understand he is a Conservative.
He votes Liberal all the same.

If I am not mistaken, I received some pri-

vale letters blaming me strongly because Mr. Green, who is not a Liberal, got the contract. I answered that Mr. Green, was the lowest tenderer, and I think that was a satisfactory answer.

Mr. Green, votes Liberal, though he is credited with being a Conservative. I have no fault to find with J. M. Green & Co. for the way in which they got the contract, if they are the lowest tenderers. It is a well known fact that the work upon armouries is largely done by bricklayers and not by carpenters. They took the contract for erecting this building for ,$29,221. The only portion of the work in which Mr. Green will be benefited is the carpenter [DOT]work, which will amount to only about $5,000, the balance of the work will be done by bricklayers. Now I have it from reliable authority that in the city of St. Thomas there is not one Liberal bricklayer. Then1 are good responsible bricklayers there, but they happen to be Conservatives, and the word has gone forth that these inen will not be allowed to lay a brick in that build-mg, for the simple reason that they are Conservatives, and for no other reason. But I understand since, that a gentleman from the cnty of London has obtained this brick work, and I suppose the reason is that he is a prominent Liberal. I say that if the gentleman who has the patronage in Elgin county is allowed to interfere to the extent of shutting out local bricklayers and bringing in men from a distance, it is goin11' pretty far.

I want to know what I can do. Mr. Green was the lowest tenderer. Whether he is a bricklayer or a carpenter, he was the lowest tenderer. We have adopted the system of giving the contract to the lowest tenderer, whoever he may be, unless there are very strong objections, as, for instance, if he happens to be well known as of bad reputation, I suppose that would be a justification for refusing him the contract'. But in the absence of any such reason the lowest tenderer has to be accepted. Then he can do as he likes, provided he delivers the goods. I cannot interfere, I cannot go to Mr. Green or anybody else and say that he must employ such and such men. i pay him the estimate when he delivers me the goods, and I have nothing else to do. Will my hon. friend tell me what else I could have done ?	'

One of the tenders was for $31,000, and the lowest was for $29,000.
I know from information from the most reliable source that Mr. Green was told that unless he would agree not to engage these local men in,- St. Thomas he would not receive the contract. I say if it has come to this pass that the parties who have the patronage in the county of Elgin can inter-

I would like to ask the hon. minister what he proposes to do with the appropriation made for the Toronto Junction public building last year. What are his intentions as to the future ?

Of course, that is not up now. It will come up in the supplementary estimates. My hon. friend (Mr. Wallace) will then, perhaps, be greatly surprised that this government do not go back on their pledges. But, my hon. friend will grant that this is not the time now to discuss the matter, because our supplementary estimates are still under consideration.

I would like to ask the hon. minister, what I have asked twice in the House before this session, what has been done with the $5,000 already appropriated ? Have the government selected a site for a public building, or have they taken any steps towards selecting that site ?

The hon. gentleman will kindly bear in mind that I was not here last year, but, the information conveyed to me is to the effect that there has been preparatory work done in the choosing of a site, but that the site has not been chosen yet. The money was voted last year in the supplementary estimates. The election came on, and we had not much time to look after these things. The case of Toronto Junction is in the same position as those of many other places. We had no time to look after them, but they will not be lost sight of.
The minister tells us that the preparatory work of selecting a site has been undertaken. What is that preparatory work ?

I have been informed of it. I did not do that preparatory work myself. I was not in the country. I believe the then acting Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Mulock) obtained some information in regard to it. I am so informed by the deputy minister.
I personally do not know anything about it, but, I may say that when the supplementary estimates come down my hon. friend will, I think, be pleased, although he is a hard man to please.

The minister tells us he was not here. Of course, we knew that, but we did not suppose that the public works of the country were going to be stopped because the minister chose to absent himself. Ten months ago. or about that time, it would be since he returned and duriug all these months the Minister of Public Works has had charge of his department, and the Postmaster General has not. He says that the Postmaster General had made some progress during the time that he was acting Minister of Public Works. That would be last May or June, or perhaps in July. How is it that nothing -has been done since that ? The minister cannot tell us of a single thing. He says that some preparatory work was done towards selecting a site. Let us hear what the nature of this preparatory work is. The minister admits that he has done nothing in regard to this matter, but that what was done was done while he was away, and done by the Postmaster General, who was acting as Minister of Public Works. I would like to know something further about this. The money has been appropriated. Parliament, voted money for the purpose. It will not do to say, because I have sought information in tiie House twice already during this session, that the matter is being considered, or that preparatory work is being done towards selecting a site. What js the nature of such preparatory work ? Have sites been proposed, have applications been made, have these matters been submitted to the department, or what is the nature of the work that has been done, or the investigations that have been made so far ? We are entitled to some information in reference to this matter, and we have no information yet except the statement of the Minister of Public Works that while he was away the Postmaster General had made some preparatory investigation. We would like to know something more about it, and to understand what the intentions of the government are in this matter.

I am very sorry indeed that I cannot give more information, because I have nothing under my hand. The deputy minister tells me that lie understood from the hon. Postmaster General that he obtained some information in reference to the site. I did not expect myself that the rostmaster General would be away from the House during this session. I fully expected that he would be here to post me as to the work done. I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) has any right to complain that time has been lost. Parliament prorogued,

the elections came on soon after, and there were a great many public works not 'started, just as this work was not started. As soon as the House prorogues, and I have time, I will certainly use my best endeavours to Push on this work and any other work for which money has been placed at my disposal. There is no secret about it, I had no time to look after a lot of things, but as soon as the House prorogues, I will pusli on the work as quickly as I can. .

I am surprised that the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) wanted an explanation about the preparatory work in connection with this public building. It is quite evident the hon. gentleman has had no public buildings erected in his constituency for some time, or he would not ask for an explanation. Perhaps the experience I have had in East Elgin may be of some assistance to the hon. gentleman if he expects a public building in his constituency.
I want to hear about it.

I will relate the preparatory work. In the first place, they buy a site and pay three prices for it to a political friend. Now, the hon. Minister of Public AVorks does not get much credit for being over-loyal. He has been attacked in this House on several occasions for being disloyal. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Taxte) saw his way clear to come from Montreal to St. Thomas the Saturday previous to the elections for the purpose of turning. the first sod of the building, although not one cent had been voted by parliament for the construction of that building.
Did it bury Wilson ?

Yes, and there is a stone there as a monument to mark his grave.
I he political friends of the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte), thought that perhaps he did not stand very well in St. Thomas, and so they sent over to London and raked and scraped all the military they could to come to St. Thomas with their bands. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) visited my opponents place, and I understand he had quite a tussle there before he could be induced to go out and turn the first sod. When he did go out, they got a very good crowd together after raking and scraping up the militia as I have said.
A corporals guard.

Yes, they got a corporals guard, and they went down and turned the first sod. After the Minister of Public Works had come all the way from Montreal to St. Thomas to turn the first sod for a building that no money had been voted for, they thought they could turn his presence to good account by holding a meeting 981	'
They combined business with pleasure.

Yes, and they got all these outsiders in to fill up the hall. Strange to say two or three little boys happened to be in the opera house and instead of going down the aisle they climbed over the seats and the Minister of Public Works was horrified to think that a gentleman from the province of Quebec could not come there to make a speech without being interrupted. The hon. gentleman (Air. Tarte) was looking for trouble that night, but the Conservative electors did not wish for a moment to put a straw in his way, and they maintained as good order as they could, so the only thing the Minister of Public AVorks could find fault with was the antics of two or three little boys. The impression given us was that the hon. gentleman came to St. Thomas especially for the purpose of trying to create some little strife in order that he might go back to the province of Quebec and say :	I have been insulted in the province of Ontario. It was for that reason and for that reason only V I have no excuse to offer for these boys, because if the King of England came there to make a speech the chances are these boys would have done' the same thing. There was nothing intended in the way of insult to the Alinister of Public AVorks.
Did he hire the boys to do it ?

No, he did not. If the Minister of Public Works is going to make it a practice to turn first sods, I would advise him not to do it the day before an election. It looks too much like making party capital out of it, and so far as our militia is concerned they will pay no heed to such a proceeding.
He did not carry the constituency.

No; the speech of the Alinister of Public Works worked the other way. I think I derived benefit from it. The hon. gentleman would have done much better in that constituency if he had stayed in the province of Quebec to assist his friends there. I have no complaint to make about the speech delivered by the hon. gentleman, and in fact I am very much obliged to him for it.

If the little speech I made there did my hon. friend (Air. Ingram) any good, I shall certainly do it again. By the way, St. Thomas [DOT] did not vote badly at all. I spoke only there, and had I spoken elsewhere I do not think that the hon. gentleman (Air. Ingram) would be here to-day. However. I might try my hand at a future election. My visit to St. Thomas was one of the most pleasant I ever made. I was very well received. There was a great military dis-

play. There was no party politics in it. 1 was invited by two military men, both of them Conservatives, to turn the first sod and I did my duty.

But nothing of the kind has, been done this past ten years, if we except the famous fence which the minister had constructed near this building. So that this large sum of $125,000 is simply for repairs in the way of carpentering, painting and furnishing. Surely that is an enormous amount for the little work of that kind that is necessary in these buildings. It amounts to nearly $375 per day. Why, a man can go around these buildings and see to-day that many of the outside sashes in the windows have not been painted in years.
We have not enough money.
Let the minister state how much of that $125,000 will be spent in carpentering work and painting and how much on furniture, and we may get some faint glimmering of where this money is to go.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. minister has made a statement which is the most misleading ever presented to this committee. I have just sent to the library to find a copy of the estimates for the years for which the hon. gentleman made up a statement. He said that the amount voted in 1887 was $175,000. I have the estimates of that year before me. It is true there is an item of $175,000 in that year. But what is it for ? We come down to the item that is covered by the vote that he is asking for here to-day 'materials for repairs, &c., in connection with ventilation and lighting of public buildings, Ottawa, $5,000.' That was the amount voted in 1887.
For this building ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yes, for just the same item.
No, no.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can send out and get the estimates.
Yes, and I will give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) a fine hat if there was ever a year when $5,000 only was voted for the purpose for which I am asking this vote. It is a joke.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is no joke. I make the statement from my place in parliament, and I read from the estimates. In 1887, the materials for repairs in connection with the ventilating and lighting was $5,000.
It was a special item.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: ' Repairs, furniture, &c., heating, &c., $15,000.' The items were voted separately, and amounted to $20,000. Now, my hon. friend is asking $125,000 for the same services that were covered in 1887 for $20,000. We have the same state of affairs in connection with the salaries for engineers, firemen, caretakers, &c. The iron, gentleman is now asking $80,000, and the amount voted in 1887 was $44,000. Every item in the estimates of 1887 was half or less than half the amount he is now asking for. If he will refer the matter to a committee, it will be shown that the statement he is trying to palm off on the House has no foundation. Let any person who understands the estimates take the estimates of the two years, and he will see that my statement is true, while the hon. gentleman's statement is misleading.

I am prepared to refer the matter to a committee. Of course, I take the statement prepared by my officer, and do not go into the books myself. I have not at hand a copy of the estimates from which my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) read, but, I know that it is out of the question, that for $5,000 these buildings could be maintained for a single year. I will look again at the estimates of 1887 to understand what the hon. gentleman has said. But, I am sure that my officers could not have made such a mistake. If my hon. friend will look at the accounts of one year, he will find that I am right in saying that every year the amounts spent on these buildings cover nearly $200,000

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, no.
There is no use in saying ' no '-it is true. My hon. friend is simply making a mistake- the thing is out of the question.
Does this item cover expenditure for telephones ?

No, that is a special vote. .1 would be very glad indeed if some responsible man from the other side of the House would come to my office-I would be glad to see him any day-and look over the details of the work done and the calls made upon us. I am sure that that would convince the hon. gentleman that the work simply could not done for less money.

There has been a great deal of discussion indulged in. But, surely, with his officers to refer to, the hon. gentleman would be able to tell us where this $125,000 is to go. It is now nearly six o'clock, and he could have the information for us after recess. We might as well vote intelligently when we are giving away $125,000.

I am ready to give all information. I

thought when I took office that the expenditure was very large, and, for months and months I followed that expenditure myself. The calls upon us are, in a sense, unforeseen. The Department of Finance, for instance, will call upon us for a change here or new furniture there, or other departments will ask for this or that. The demands upon us are at times surprising, and if we complied with them all, instead of spending $125,000 we should spend $250,000 a year. I can show dozens of letters from my colleagues, complaining that I do not give them what they require. All those who have been in large business know what it costs to keep up large buildings, and these buildings are immense. God knows how many chairs are broken every day, and how many desks need to be repaired or changed, or how many carpets or tables must be procured. I had no conception, before I took office, that I should have so much trouble in keeping up buildings.

It is plain that the minister will be in a position to-night to furnish us approximately with these expenditures. In the meantime, it may be worth while to quote some figures from the Auditor General's Report, which will show where some of the public money goes. The Minister of Public Works tells us to look at the Auditor General's Report to learn what the expenditures are, but it is not easy, at a moment's notice, to go over all these figures. Perhaps we may judge of the rest of the expenditures by a few that happen to have struck my eye. There are no gentlemen now on the other side such as those who used to rail about public expenditure.
What has become of them ?

The people have got rid of them, and they have gone to their reward. Those sitting behind the ministers now have no condemnation for anything that the Minister of Public Works may do. They are all dangling after votes for harbours, for docks to be built at places that cannot be approached, and petty grants of all kinds. We know how, in the days of Sir John Macdonald, hon. gentlemen used to rail at the expenditure of a few dollars for cab hire. But, let us see how these princes of the blo'od royal live at the public expense. Take, for instance, the Department of the Interior. The Minister of the Interior wants a telephone in his house. Of course, he should pay for his own telephone, to order any household supplies that he wants, but he asks parliament to vote that a telephone be supplied to him. And the deputy minister asks for a telephone also, and that must be provided at the public expense. Then, the private secretary cannot go down town to order his own groceries, and he asks that a telephone be installed in his house at the expense of the
country. And there is Mr. Pedley, a very ambitious gentleman, who used to be heard throughout the country. He is going to be as good as his master, and he asks for a telephone, which is put in and paid for by the public, go, it would appear that the ministers, deputy ministers, leading clerks, and clerks that are not leading clerks, have telephones installed in their houses, and the country pays the piper. How does the Minister of Public Works stand up in the House to-day and tell us that we should pay for, a telephone for these different subordinate clerks in the departments, and, furthermore, that he is going to let it run down to a subordinate clerk like Mr. Pedley Are the messengers in the service to have the same favour extended to them in the coming year ? Now, if this telephone abuse is going on, how bad must be the abuse in the expenditure of $125,000 ? I think before this side of the House will permit this item to pass, the minister must obtain from his officer approximate information to show us how this $125,000 is to be spent, how much is to be expended on repairs on the buildings, and what expenditures will be entered upon during the coming year.

I must take issue with my hon. friend. He has only to look again at what he has read to find that he is mistaken in his interpretation. Let me read it : ' Material for repairs, &c., being in connection with the ventilation and lighting of public buildings, Ottawa, $5,000,' especially mentioning ventilation. Now, this does not cover repairs, furniture, &c.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Take the next item right under that.

Will the hon. gentleman give me time to explain matters, matters that are clear in themselves, but that need explanation after what the hon, gentleman has said. This was a special vote in connection with ventilation and lighting of public buildings.
Mr. TAYLOR, It is only material used for them.

For ventilation and lighting, that is all, a special item. Hon. gentlemen on both sides can read for themselves what I am reading now on this page : Material for repairs, &c., in connection with ventilation and lighting of public buildings, Ottawa.' ' Material for repairs '-it was a special item then. Since then we have simply merged into the general expenditure that small vote; but for the very same year, 1897, there was a sum of $175,000 for repairs, furniture, heating public buildings in Ottawa. That is the whole thing in these two items.

Would the minister, after six o'clock, kindly bring down a detailed

statement about this $125,000? We should expect to have that information.

I must explain that it is impossible to give details of that kind. I will not undertake to do what I cannot do. The broad lines of the expenditure are contained in the Auditor General's account. These are the expenditures every year. My officers have been there twenty years, and they know that about the same expenditure has been made every year, except that it was more in the past. I cannot be expected to say to the House that a little piece of wall in some particular place will have to be rebricked, or that so many tables will have to be bought, or that the Auditor General will ask for a counter. I cannot do that. If the House does not trust the Department of Public Works, well, I would like to know what we are to do. I will give every possible information, but there are things that cannot be expected. Now, Sir, as to the telephones. My hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) will permit me-I am an older man than himself-to give him one word of advice. He has ability ; he does not gain anything by small criticisms like that. The telephone system has been established all over the world in profusion ; so much so that in large firms in cities they have a pri-yate telephone system with which they communicate to all their employees. Take large newspapers like the Star, La Patrie, La Presse, I am sure that in those offices there are forty or fifty telephones which communicate with all the branches of the concern. Suppose I am working in my new house- 'which I am sorry to say I have to do so often that I do not know whether I will work very much longer here-suppose I have to go at ten o'clock at night and open my letters, or in the morning, and open my letters in my room, or at night after the House has adjourned, if I want to communicate with my deputy minister, or with my private secretary, or if I want to speak to one of my colleagues, can I not have a telephone by which I can do so ? It is a saving of time, it is in the public interest, and I say without hesitation we have not enough telephones now. I am asking for more money this year. My hon. friend himself may be a minister some of these days, and I can tell him that in indulging in criticisms of this kind he will find out that he has made a mistake, both in the interest of his party and in his own interest. Let him reflect a little. Why should we grant telephones without any necessity ? There is no pleasure in doing so, I do not get any advantage from granting a telephone ; I do so because I think it is in the public interest.
The Minister of Public Works has undertaken to read me a lecture on the ground of my talking ' small talk.' I have this to say of the Minister of Public Works, that the man who criticises such

scandalous expenditure as this is considerably bigger than the man who makes the expenditure and who is so small as to ask the country to pay for it. This thing shows that the men who are in positions to-day on the treasury benches, go about the country treating their friends In a lavish way with wines, liquors and cigars, and afterwards come down and ask the country to pay for them.
Who does that ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies).

speechtext: It is not in his department. I think the Minister of Marine and Fsiheries is too big to do that work.
It is not in mine either.
It is in the items, and it will be shown before this session is through.
These expenditures he is talking about are not included in this.

I did not say they were in his department, I say they are in the Auditor General's Report, and will be referred to before the session is over.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before recess, I was asked to give some information as to the nature of the expenditure. I stated that it was impossible to give any details. I have met my officers since, and they tell me that about $60,000 in round numbers, perhaps a little more, have to be paid in wages. The balance is employed to buy new furniture; materials and so on. The Auditor General's Report contains all the expenditure for every year that has elapsed since confederation. By noting that expenditure in past years one can form an idea as to what the expenditure of this year will be. It is always about the same thing. We have several buildings, the Central Building, the West Block, the East Block, the Langevin Block, the Supreme Court building, the Geological Museum, the National Art Gallery and the Printing Bureau. All these buildings are large, and expensive to keep up. Of course, it is out of the question for any minister to follow day by day how many pounds of nails are used, how many chairs are broken, how many panes of glass have to be put in again, how many yards of paint have to be done. The work is under the supervision of the chief architect, Mr. Ewart, an employee of thirty years' standing of the Public Works Department. I have full confidence in him. There is Mr. Breton, who is foreman of the men, and an old employee, and

there is Mr. Ellis, who is foreman of the shops, and also an old employee. 1 have kept the whole staff, which is responsible for the expenditure, and which was there before I took office. I have kept the very same men there. I am sure that they do not expend money uselessly. I am sure that they are doing their duty to the best of their ability. More than that, I cannot say.

Does the hon. minister mean to say that these men, such as Mr. Ewart and the others whom he has mentioned, order goods from whomsoever they wish, or does he give instructions from whom they must purchase supplies ?

The supplies, which in this ease amount to about one-third of the expenditure, are bought. I must say frankly, after competition, from the political friends of the party now in office-not exclusively though. I am often reproached, and once or twice I have been censured by my own friends, because they thought I was not partisan enough. Some of them believe that I should have dismissed the whole staff. I did not do so. I do not believe in that kind of business. When a man does his duty, I believe he has a right to stay. I speak of the heads. Materials are bought as much as possible from the friends of the party in office, as it was done years ago, and as it will be done when we are out of office.
I see, according to the Auditor General's Report, that there were some supplies got from Mr. W. G. Charleson. Is that the same gentleman who was before the Public Accounts Committee the other day ?
Yes.
Can the hon. gentleman tell me how much was paid to him last year ?

No. I cannot say how much we paid him. Perhaps I may take this opportunity of saying that although the prices paid to him are fair, I think that my officers bought too much from that man. I think that other friends should have received more patronage than they have in the past, although I have nothing to say against Mr. Charleson. I believe his prices are fair, but I think perhaps a little too much has been bought from him from the party's standpoint. because after all, it is a family quarrel. My hon. friends must not expect, now that they are out of office, that they will get patronage at our hands. That would not be fair. Of course, they would not take it.
Can the hon. minister give us any idea how much they paid him ?
Between $5,000 and $6,000, so I am informed. I did not look into, the figures.

Of course, I have not been able to go very largely into the Auditor General's Report, but I see here some $8,000 that this man got in two or three buildings.
j The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. It may be.

It seems to me ' that this is a very large amount for one man to get. The hon. minister makes the statement that his prices are fair, but I think his prices are most unreasonable. This gentleman, the other day, explained that he only started business in 1898, and that the government were customers to the extent of 50 per cent of his business. It seems a very strange thing that this man should furnish such a large quantity of these supplies. I, personally, think it looks rather suspicious, and I was wondering whether the officers of the department were really the ones that were responsible for dealing with this man, or whether it was the minister himself who would issue orders like that. I could hardly believe that any officer of the government would attempt to give any one man orders for such a large quantity of supplies as that. Now, another thing that I am really surprised at is this:
; I have been coming to Ottawa now myself, j for nine years, and if there has been any large amount of expenditure out of this $125,000 I on this building, in which we now are, it cannot be seen in any place. I was looking around this evening after we had left the House. I think the buildings around here are in a most disgraceful state, and if there is to be $125,000 spent every year we should have the assurance of the minister that this building will be put in better shape than it is in at the present time. The hon. minister must admit that when he goes through these corridors they are hardly fit for any person to be in at all. I do not believe they have been painted since the building was erected. The oilcloth and everything around them is in a disgraceful condition, and yet, there is $125,000 to be expended. I cannot see where the $125,000 goes to. Then, the hon. minister has told us that $60,000 are paid in wages. That represents at least $200 per day. There must be eighty or ninety men at work on these repairs. I think these public buildings should be kept in proper order with $125,000. According to the Auditor General's Report only $3,000 : of the expenditure reached this building that we are now in. I think we should have the assurance of the minister that there shall be more attention paid to this building than has been given to it in the past.

The ventilation of this building is pretty bad still. I would

like some information as to how much of this $125,000 is for the purpose of ventilation.	.

This money does not apply to the improvement of the ventilation, because I think the old system is radically bad. In this House we are simply locked up in these walls. The ventilation comes from beneath the floor and we cannot change it. 1 hope that in a short time the House will vote the money necessary to change the whole system. Anybody who compares the conditions with the necessities of the public service, anybody who has been some time here and who has looked carefully into the question must admit that a change has to come. There is no room; there is no space. I have heard my hon. friends criticising me because I have rented buildings outside. There is no pleasure in that. The buildings here are congested, and I suppose they will have to be changed some of these days. We do not know where to put our books in the library. I am not prepared to offer any plans now, but within a short time we will be obliged to devise a scheme between ourselves to change the whole thing, and then I hope we will have better ventilation. We are here for four or five months of the year and I agree that we should have better accommodation. The ventilation is better than it was before we introduced the new lighting system.

From 1882 to 1892 when the House was lit by gas, the atmosphere in the evening became intolerable and the ventilation was then a burning question. The ventilation of the House is not so bad now in view of the improvements made within the last five or six years. When the summer days come, the windows are now removed and the Chamber is a paradise compared with what it was. I do not know of any large chamber in which you have any better ventilation under the improved system.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not agree with the minister (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) that the ventilation is good. I think the ventilation of the Chamber is very bad indeed.
So it is.
One would think that the system had been devised to keep the air as bad as possible and to secure as many draughts as possible.
I think we have now the best ventilation possible under the circumstances.

Since six o'clock the minister has given us information which he failed to give us before, and perhaps now Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
we may get on with the estimates. The minister tells us that there will be an expenditure next year of $60,000 for wages in maintaining the public buildings here. That means that about 175 men will be employed every working day in the year.
At what wages ?

At about $1.50 a day. That is quite a small army to keep amused because they cannot be kept at work all the year round. The minister estimates that there will be an addition of about $40,000 in materials and furniture. It appears from the Auditor General's Report that the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) supplied one folding bed last year with the proper equipment. Who was that for ?

Last year I was very ill as everybody knows and I had a folding bed in my room in the buildings. If parliament cannot afford to supply that to a sick minister, I am prepared to pay for it; but I do not think the House will go to that extreme. I was very near dying last year. I sat late in the House here when I should have been away, and I had a folding bed put in my room.
Before dinner the minister invited us to look at the Auditor General's Report, and I saw this item and I wondered who it was for.
It was for me. I ordered a very modest folding bed which is in my room and which will be there for the use of my successor.
Is ice supplied to all the officers ?
Yes.

At page 103 of the Auditor General's Report it appeared that J. O. Charlebois was paid $42 for ice for the Hon. Mr. Sifton. Was he sick or unduly warm, because I do not see that any other minister was suffering to the extent of having to be supplied with $42 worth of ice.

Some departments take ice in the winter and some do not. Those who want ice in the winter months have it and those who do not want it do not have it. I do not think there is any very great crime in paying $42 for ice in the year. I do not think the electors of the country will be very much influenced by the purchase of a folding bed for a sick minister and for ice for the Department of the Interior.

The minister invited criticism on these items, and as I did not know that the Minister of Public Works was so ill as to require a folding bed and that the Minister of the Interior wanted ice, when I saw tlie items here they excited my curi-

osity. It is to be hoped that there will be no rivalry on the part of other ministers to cause them, to buy winter ice also. How that the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has come down from his high horse and consented to give us information which should have been given before, so far as I am concerned, I will not oppose these items. The Minister of Public Works must understand that if he hopes to have his estimates passed he cannot take the high and mighty course that he did before six o'clock, and that it is better for him to do as he has done since, namely, play the meek and innocent minister.

I do not believe that I deserve that criticism. I always endeavour to be courteous towards members on both sides of the House and to give Information cheerfully. I believe that a minister should be at the disposal of the House to give information. Let me tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) that he is altogether mistaken as to the wages we pay our men here. As a rule we pay union wages and instead of the average of $1.50 a day which he calculates, our carpenters receive as a rule $2 a day. Painters are paid $2.50 and even $3 a day at times, and bricklayers $3 at times. We are paying union wages. I am sure there is no money wasted. There may be some little trouble here and there, as there is in the best regulated establishments, but as a rule I believe my officers do their duty loyally and faithfully.
According to the Auditor General's Report, the total wages paid last year were $90,575.24. Does the minister mean that this year there will be a reduction of $30,000 in wages ?
I am sure my hon. friend is mistaken. There could not have been $90,000 in wages paid for the maintenance of the buildings last year ; for I had a vote of only $100,000 altogether.

According to the Auditor General's Report, the total amount paid on account of Ottawa buildings-repairs, furniture, &c., was $148,526.85. In that $105,382 was paid for wages, less $14,806, leaving the net amount of wages paid $90,575.
