The chief architect tells me that this year he does not expect to pay in wages more than $60,000. My hon. friend will find that the amount he has given covers renewals, repairs, rents, &c., of Ottawa and other buildings.
It is under the heading which I have given and I cannot see one item of rent in it.

If my hon. friend looks at the foot note, he will find that in. this total of $148,526 the amount of $27,865 is for bills due before the 1st of July. I may say that when I took office there were bills overdue ; and for years the Department of Public Works has always been in debt. I have made up my mind to put a stop to that state of affairs, to make a clean breast of the whole thing, and come straight to this House and tell them that we cannot keep up these buildings with $100,000.
I understand that previous to this the same system has been going on, of adding to the expenditure of the year amounts due previously.
It lias been going on for fifteen years. It Is a bad system.

Admitting that there was $27,865 from the previous year included in the $148,526, and deducting that, then the total expenditure of the past year has been $121,000. Therefore the minister lias exceeded the amount voted by at least $21,000. Am I right in that ?

No. I was not here last year, but my officers tell me that we got a vote of $100,000, and afterwards an additional vote of $23,000. Then there were bills due for $27,000. In point of fact, the Department of Public Works for the last fifteen years has expended more than it has got from this parliament. This year I made up my mind to make a clean breast of it ; and next year, if I am here, I pledge myself that there will not be one dollar of over-expenditure.
If my memory serves me rightly, we had the same explanation last year. Some minister came forward and made a clean breast of it in the same way.
I understand last year there was not a woid of debate.

It may not have been on the Public Works estimates, but it certainly was on some of the estimates, because I was present and heard it. Do I understand from the minister that there will be no amount from the previous year charged in this $125,000 ?

I would not say that. We are in debt now. The appropriation has been short for years, but with this amount of money I will pay my debts, and will not incur any new debts. I pledge myself to this House not to make any new debts, if I am here.
If the minister is not here, how are we to hold the government responsible ?
The Minister of Public Works never dies.
It seems to me that the kon. minister proposes to spend about $05,000 on furniture and other supplies.
No. The bon. gentleman has misunderstood me. Repairs to old furniture, and buying new furniture will not cover more than $25,000 or $50,000.

I am sorry to hear that because I had hopes that the hon. gentleman was going to make a new venture which is very desirabe. I thought be was going to provide better accommodation for members by giving them private rooms and furnishing them so that at least every three or four members would have a room where they could do their clerical work and study. I had hopes that with tbe large sum at bis disposal, he would have made some provision along tbe line I have indicated, and thus avoid the necessity for the complaints we have had in the past.
In the supplementaries for next year, the hon. gentleman will find an item providing for the accommodation so much required.
We are all very glad to hear it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. the minister before recess gave the House a statement of the cost of public buildings at Ottawa from 1S82 to 1880-7, and in 1887, he said, the amount was $175,000 which was voted. I do not remember the amount he said was spent. I sent to the library and got the estimates for that year, and in those estimates the words ' public buildings, Ottawa,' do not appear in the item he read, and the hon. gentleman was misleading the House.
I said it was for Ottawa.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman read what was printed in the book, and the words ' public buildings, Ottawa,' are not opposite that item, though they are opposite every item that refers to these public buildings, such as removing stoves, heating, electric light, telephonic service, salaries of engineers, firemen and caretakers. This $175,000 includes buildings outside Ottawa. If the hon. gentleman will take the estimates he will find one charge for $5,000. and another for $15,000, under the same heading as ' repairs, furniture, heating, Ac., public buildings, Ottawa.' The words ' public buildings. Ottawa,' are not in the estimates which he read at all. but are to be found in the items lower down.

I did not mislead the House. I read a statement covering over twenty years, which proves that every year there has been an Mr. REID (Grenville).
expenditure varying from $220,000 per year to $125,000 for the maintenance of these buildings in Ottawa. We have spent in some years $150,000, and in others $200,000, and this year we spent a little less. And in those days we had not as many public buildings, although we spent more. For instance, we had not the Langevin block.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In the Auditor General's Report for 1897-8, I have seen that $175,000 was expended, but it appears it was expended on public buildings generally and not on public buildings in Ottawa. My hon. friend must admit that when he read from this book, he read * repairs, furniture and heating, public buildings, Ottawa, $175,000,' yet those words ' public buildings, Ottawa,' are not in the vote at all.

What I mean is this. When $25,000 additional were asked by my officers, I asked them to give me some reason for the increase. Then they prepared this statement which reads : ' Public buildings, Ottawa,' and I read it as they gave it. My officers still tell me that the money was spent in that way, but supposing that in 1887 there was a mistake, that would not prove at all that the amount was excessive.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend need not again try to mislead the House, because he did not read from the paper, but from the book, and he read $175,000 for public building at Ottawa, when the words ' public buildings at Ottawa.' do not appear in the item he read. Further down, he will find the item just as he has it, ' material for repairs, Ac., in connection with the ventilation and lighting of public buildings at Ottawa. $5,000.' ' Repairs, furniture, heating, &e., $15,000.' If he says the $175,000 applied to public buildings everywhere, he must add this $5,000 and $15,001, which would make $190,000. The hon. gentleman had the book before him when he quoted the figures, and he should be man enough-
Order.
It is no use talking that way ; I believe I am something of a man. When I make a mistake, I am ready frankly to admit it. But I do not believe I was mistaken.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If the bon. gentleman will take the book I have here and read the item as it is printed, he will see that he is wrong and he must admit that he misled the House-or tried to.

I did not mislead the House. My officers gave me a statement, which I read. My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) has sent me a book lirecting my attention to certain items which I also read. But I do not see wherein what I stated was wrong. But in any case, what do I care whether they spent $15,000 more

or less in 1887 ? I was not there, nor was my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I will ask the hon. minister to allow this item to stand and I will meet his officer, and, if it is not shown that the statement the hon. gentleman read was a [DOT] misleading one, there will be no further delay in passing the item so far as I am concerned.
This seems to me a most unfair proposition to make. Why should the passing of this item depend on what was spent in 1887
Why did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) make the statement if there was no objection in it ?
I did not make it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am satisfied that ' Hansard ' will prove to-morrow that my hon. friend read from the estimate of 1887 ' repairs, furniture, heating, &c., public buildings, Ottawa, $175,000.'

If I understand the hon. gentleman, he says that I read this item as $175,000 for Ottawa. I do not think I read it so, but I may have done so ; and, if I did, I have no hesitation in saying that I made a mistake. Surely, I cannot say more than that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I will ask the hon, gentleman to allow this item to stand, and I will prove to his officer that he made a mistake in putting that statement into the minister's hands, and that the amount that I have quoted was granted in the years stated for the same services as the hon, gentleman is now asking $175,000 for.

We must make some progress in the estimates. There is nothing material in this statement after all. I will give every chance to discuss the matter, for I have nothing to hide. If I have misled the House or the hon. gentleman, I will be the first to admit it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman comes down with a prepared statement to show that the late government spent much larger sums annually than he is spending, and when he comes down to the last year of that administration he says the government starved the public buildings. But when we go back to other years and study the figures for these services, we find that the accounts had been changed. But the Auditor General's Report gives the details of the items, and a careful study of them will show that no such sum was spent for repairs and furniture for the public buildings as shown on the statement the hon. gentleman has given. I am prepared to meet the hon. gentleman's officer and convince him that he has placed an erroneous statement
in the minister's hands. And it was placed there for the purpose of showing that the late government spent more than, the present government has been spending, whereas the fact is that he has increased it from 25 to 50 per cent, and in some cases even 100 per cent.

as I said, we shall have plenty of time to discuss these matters. I have placed the figures before the House as prepared by the accountant of the department. Let the item pass and I will undertake that every opportunity will be given for discussion.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do not know how far we are justified in accepting these statements. The hon. minister promised a meeting of the Public Accounts Committee to deal with another matter, but we are not to have a meeting.
I understand there is to be a meeting.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have had no notice of it.
Why not ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do not know.
I do not know either-Oh, yes, I believe there is to be a caucus to-morrow. But I will pledge myself to this-that this meeting shall be held.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: A vote for the same service appears in the supplementary estimates for this year, and before that item comes up, I must have this statement revised by the Auditor General's Report of the expenditures for each year.

I will send a copy of the statement to my hon. friend.
Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Public Buildings-Rents, repairs, furniture, heating, &c. -Rents-Dominion public buildings, $31,000.
There is an increase of $10,000 here. Will the hon. minister explain that and state what these rents are for.
It is for rentals for new buildings-the Sey-bold building, the Department of Labour and the building for the Interior Department.
Are these rents for buildings in Ottawa only ?
No, throughout the country.
Has the hon. gentleman a list showing how this $10,000 is made up ?
A list has been prepared, and I will supply
Why not let the item stand in the meantime ? We would like to know where these rented buildings are.

I have here a list covering three pages. I hope hon. gentlemen do not expect me to read it. I must say that my physical strength will not allow me to do that. I would rather throw up the sponge and let the item go. But I will place it on the Table. It may look like obstruction not to read it, but I cannot do it.
Let the item stand for fifteen minutes so that we may have a new building-included in this list?
Is the building on the corner of Metcalfe and Slater streets-the new building-included in this list ?
Yes.
What is the rent of it ?
What is the rent of the Se.vbold building ?
Then the whole increase of the rents appearing in the estimates this year over and above last year, is the rent of those two buildings?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, I do not ask through curiosity anything in reference to the rental of those buildings, but I have been requested to do so by a number of gentlemen representing both sides of politics who are not satisfied with the policy of the government in renting so many of our fine buildings, and at the same time withdrawing them from contributing to the city revenues to the extent of $31,000. This sum appearing in the estimates to-day for rental if capitalized at 5 per cent, represents $600,000 worth of property. That means to the city of Ottawa, at 2 per cent, $12,000, independent of water rates. I am well aware that the government have dealt with tolerable liberality with the city a year or two ago by giving them $60,000. But when giving this $60,000 the government withheld from the city all improvements on Wellington street, on Sappers and Duffenin bridges, on the Maria street bridge, and also on the slide bridges, and also $15,000 which the city got annually from the government for water supplied to the buildings. All these amounts have been taken from the city exchequer. Doubtless a good many members of this House think that this $60,000 was a donation to the city, and | Mr. TARTE.
that the city gives nothing to the government in return. I would like to tell those hon. gentlemen that there is no money the government has invested, either this government or any preceding government, that returns better value than that money given to the city. If these buildings were assessed the same as any ordinary buildings, assessed we will say, the same as Ontario buildings are, which is one-third less than the actual value, this government would have, to pay the city $40,000 for water rates alone. The assessment is about $10,000,000, take one-third off for exemption, and the balance would represent a taxation of $40,000 for water rates. Then take the exemption by the government of the civil service income tax, which amounts to about a million dollars, that would be $20,000, which makes up the $60,000 which the government donates the city independent of the water supply to the experimental farm, the fisheries, the geological museum and the bureau, those are still exempt, the city receives nothing more. Now it seems to me that if it pays individuals to erect buildings for the government, why would it not pay the government to expend their own money to erect buildings for themselves on their own property ? (I do not wish to find fault with the government in renting buildings ; what I find fault with is that in renting buildings, which I suppose are the best quality of buildings, they immediately become exempt from taxation, and so many dollars are withdrawn from the city exchequer. Now I have the opinion of a very careful contractor who stated to me that this building about which so much has been said could be altered for about $250,000, so as to concentrate all the offices throughout the city and make them much more handy and convenient. At the same time we would have, as has been said this evening, an office or a room where, if a friend came to see us on private business, we could take him. As it is now there is no place for us to go to unless it is into a little alcove in the library, and if we sit down at the table the chances are that some person comes in and sits down at the same table. That is not as it should be. We ought to have some place where we would be able to meet a friend and talk over matters with some degree of privacy. As I have said, I do not wish to find any fault with the government in renting buildings, nor yet do I want to find fault with the gentlemen who have buildings to rent to the government. At the same time we must look to the public interest. I notice that in 1896 the rents were only $12,397 ; in 1898 the rents were $14,852 ; in 1900, $21,buu and for the present year $31,000. Now it seems to me that if this matter is allowed to go on there is no knowing where it will end. The first thing we know we will have no *revenue coming in from the central part *of the city at all. I would ask the government to consider a report that was sent in

by a sub-committee appointed by the Privy Council in the fall of 1892, and which was handed in to the Privy Council on the 3rd of January, 1893. If the government will act upon this report, so far as I am concerned, I will be perfectly satisfied, because I think the government are inclined to do what is right and just by the city, I think they are trying to help us as much as they can. So far as the action of the government tends to deplete the taxes coming into the city treasury, I presume it is from want of thought more than anything else. The portion of the sub-committee's report which I wish to read is the following :
That instructions be given to all the departments to make no covenant or stipulation in any lease hereafter made as to the payment of taxes by the Crown, and that in all leases or lettings by the Crown there shall be a stipulation that the lessees shall pay taxes to the city; also that copies of this be sent to all the departments.
Mr. Chairman, I hope that, having drawn this matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works, he will give it that attention that the sub-committee referred to required should be given.

I fully sympathize with what has been said by my hon. friend. The system which we have been following is altogether wrong. We have been renting right and left, hut we were hound to do so. Space was necessary, it had to be obtained, and we could not help ourselves. The great trouble is that when the Minister of Public Works comes before his colleagues, or comes before the House to ask for money, he is looked upon as a sort of public enemy, everybody is down on him, he is spending too much. Well, if I had my own way I would no doubt follow the policy that has just been suggested. This year my hon. friend will find in the estimates that we are beginning to do what he has advocated. I hope we will be able to start work on the museum, which is a most necessary work indeed. We have taken risks' that no government should have taken-I do not speak of this government alone, but of all governments. We are going to try to make up for lost time. What is the plan to be adopted,
I am not prepared to say to-day. When the estimates come down I will be prepared to offer some suggestions and to state my views. But I fully sympathize with what my hon. friend has said. It is quite true that every building we rent is so much withdrawn from the taxation and from the city >
revenue, and dt is not fair from the point of view of the city. At the same time, the ho>n. gentleman will admit that this government has not been unkind to the city of Ottawa. We have done things that no past government lias done, and I hope that even "my hon. friend will not forget us in his
prayers. I think we should all be proud of this city. This is the capital of the Dominion. We should do everything we can, without spending too much money, to make it a worthy capital of the great country that Canada is.
Could the hon. minister tell me how many buildings the government have rented in Ottawa now ?
Well, the list is in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite.
There is only one list; we cannot all have it.
My officers cannot say exactly. It is all in the list. It is in the hands of my hon. friends on the other side of the House.
Can yon get it all down on one sheet of paper ?
There is the list which I put on the Table of the House. I think we have six buildings rented.
Could the hon. minister tell me the date when the Seybold building was rented at $6,000 a year ?
In December, last, I understand.

Well then, I will call the attention of the hon. minister to the fact that on the 5th March he came down to the House and asked for $10,000 to spend on that building. On that afternoon there was a very lengthy discussion. It was stated that the Seybold building had been sold for $20,000, and I think it was also stated that the assessment of that building by the city of Ottawa was upwards of $40,000. On that occasion the hon. minister assured the House that the rent was $3,500 a year, and the whole contention that afternoon was, that, in view of the fact that the government was spending $10,000 on the building, that rental of $3,500 a year was too much. It cannot he that there was a typographical error or that the minister was misunderstood on that occasion in stating it at $3,500 a year, because I find on page after page of ' Hansard,' different hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House referred to the fact that the rental was $3,500 a year. In the face of the positive statement of the minister on the 5th of March, that the rent of that building was $3,500 a year, how is it that he now states it to he $6,500 a year ?

I cannot understand it. I did not correct the proofs. I may say that I do not correct the proofs of statements I make in the debate on the estimates. I cannot understand how that statement is there. My

officers were here and it was well known to me that the rental was $6,500 a year. X cannot understand how that statement Is there because there was nothing to hide. It was a public act. There was a deed signed. My officers were here. Surely I had no idea of deceiving the House.

I would inform the hon. minister that in the report of ' Hansard ' on the discussion of that day, I see no mention of the fact of a lease having been executed, but I find it spread over several pages that hon. gentlemen, all afternoon, referred to the fact that the rent was to be $3,500.
I found that out myself.

Well, in the face of that statement, the minister sits here all afternoon, he hears the discussion going on, he hears the statement made as to the value of the building, he hears the contention put forth as to the amount which was to be expended on the building, $10,000, he hears what is said as to the value of the building, as it had been assessed by the city of Ottawa, and he hears the contention of the members of the committee that $3,500 for that building is a high rental. Now, the minister comes down and tells us that the rental is not $3,500, but $6,500. The minister cannot rely upon the fact that it is a typographical error, because there has been no error at all. -ill through the debate, a debate lasting for a considerable length of time, reference was made to the fact that there was to be an expenditure of $10,000 on the building and that the rental was to be $3,500. The minister sat here that afternoon and heard those statements and now that the vote is being put through for .the rental the minister changes his whole front and says that instead of the rental being $3,500 a year it is $6,500 a year. It was stated that afternoon that this building, which is the property of a gentleman who is very prominent in the ranks of hon. gentlemen opposite in this city, was assessed for $40,000, that it had been sold a little time before for $20,000, that $10,000 was a very large expenditure to benefit that building by way of repairs and that $3,500 was a large rental on that investment. Now. the minister comes down and does not ask for the amount that he assured the House would be the rental, but he tells us that the rental is $6,500 a year. Once again I repeat that the minister cannot rely on the fact that there has been a typographical error because that afternoon the whole discussion went upon the basis that the rental was $3,500 a year. It seems to me a most extraordinary thing that after assuring the House that he had made a contract for $3,500 a year, he comes down and says that the rental is to be double that, or $6,500 a year.

I cannot say more than this that I do not know how I got mixed up. I knew very well that it was $6,500 a year. My two officers who are here to-night were sitting by me then. They knew that better than 1 did because they had made the bargain themselves. I cannot understand how that misstatement has been made here. Surely I cannot be accused of any intention of hiding it. It is a public affair, a public transaction. I cannot understand it. I suppose that my hon. friend may have made slips.
I may have made a slip, I must admit, and a bad one, but there cannot be any evil intention in it, because it is such a clear case.
1 could not hide it if I had any intention to do so, which I had not. When somebody called my attention to it I said :	Surely I
did not say $3,500 because I knew it was not that. I suppose I got mixed up because we * paid $3,500 for the Interior Department. I do not know how I did it, but I did it. I cannot deny it.

The hon. minister stated on that day that they were paying $3,500 a year for three years, and that they proposed to expend $10,000 in repairs on that building.
It is the intention of the minister to spend $10,000 and to pay $6,500 a year besides ?

The department is obliged to spend a large amount of money for the requirements of the census. The census could not be postponed. We had no other place that we could find that would suit. The Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher), myself and his officers, and my officers put their heads together with the result that we rented that . building. We had no accommodation elsewhere and we rented it. We are responsible for it. I do not believe that the rent is too high, although I grant it is high. In Ottawa things are pretty high. It is just as it is in British Columbia at times. Sometimes I think we are in British Columbia.

Are we to understand that when the hon. minister made this lease in December last, it was for $6,506 a year for three years instead of $3,500. and that the department is to expend $10,000 for repairs ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: For what term has the hon. minister rented the building that is being put up at the corner of Metcalfe and Slater streets ?
For ten years.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: At $3,500 a year ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is the building to cost ?

I cannot say. The Department of the Interior require the accommodation for the surveyor general. The officers of that department started negotiations in this matter.
>Ir. TAYLOR. Did the minister agree to pay $3,000 a year without knowing the cost of the building ?
There is not only the cost of the building, but the cost of the site.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understand that the site cost $1,000 and the building is to cost $12.000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I am credibly informed that the owners bought the site for $1,000 and have a contract let for $12,000 for the common plain building they are putting up You have rented the Seybold building for $0,500 a year for three years and you are to spend $10,000 for improving it, which improvements will revert to the owner at the end of the three years. In all you pay Sev-bold $29,500 for the three years. The gov eminent knew that the census had to be * taken and why did they not put up a building of their own for that $29,500. This is simply giving the money of the people to political friends. In another similar job you pay $3,000 a year for ten years as rent for a building that I am credibly informed will cost $12,000. That is the way the Minister of Public Works is doing business for the people of this country who entrust him 'VI,1 "*eir money. He makes this contract without consulting parliament or anybody else and lie pays his political friends exorbitant rents. I do not wonder at my hon. mend (Mr. Birkett), who represents the citv complaining that under this system the government is robbing the municipality of Ottawa ot' taxation it properly should receive. If this $29,o00 were expended on a building erected on a site near the printing bureau you would have proper accommodation for your census work, and when that was done the building would belong to the government and could be used as an addition to the printing bureau.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS Me have agreed to pay $3,000 a year for ten years for a building to accommodate the Surveyor General. That had to be done without the authority of parliament because the Ottawa Bank gave notice that the Surveyor General would have to leave the office which he has occupied for a good many years before we took office and for which we paid $1,800 a year. The Surveyor General had to get accommodation to do his 99
work, and I did what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) or any other business man would do, namely, to secure offices for him before the 1st of May. I could not do anything else. As to the Seybold building I could not help myself either. The census of Canada had to be carried on from the 1st of April and there was no time to wait. What is the use of saying we are adding $10,000 to the value of that building ? We were obliged to make partitions and elevators and so on to accommodate our census officers, and that will not add much to the Intrinsic value of the building. I am prepared to stand censure front hon. gentlemen opposite because I provided for this national work, but I believe the people of Canada will understand there was nothing else for me to do.

The criticism is not because the minister has secured the buildings. but it is because he is paying too much rent for these buildings and spending too much money on them. According to the minister's own figures this building will cost $5,000 for the site and $12,010 for the buildings, or in all $17,000.
They will cost more than that.

The man who rents that building for $3,000 makes from 18 to 20 per cent on his investment. That is a good investment for the citizen of Ottawa who rents to the government but it is a very poor investment for the country. It would be far better for the government to erect their own buildings.
I grant all that.
Surely it is not necessary for the government to pay such high rents.
In Dawson City the rent for the commissioner will be $300 a month this year, and it appears to have been $1,200 a month last year.

The Department of the Interior, I suppose through Mr. Ogilvie, has re-rented these buildings and as the Department of Public Works pays the rente the bills have simply been sent to us. However, that state of affairs will not last long in Dawson. We have one building ready and another building is being erected now. and when the estimates come down my hon. friend will find that we take a vote to provide ourselves with a home in Dawson.

I think the Minister of Public Works misunderstood me; a moment ago. I was not finding fault with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tarte) or with the government for renting any building in or about the city of Ottawa, nor with the rent they are paying. Neither was I finding any fauit



3 HO
with what the government has done for the city. On the contrary, I give them credit for doing as much as we reasonably could expect. But what I am finding fault with is this. The government in all cases is a good enough tenant to enable the landlord to pay the taxes. So long as we get the taxes, we do not care what the government pay in a reasonable way ; and if they would stipulate that all leases made in the future should provide for the payment of taxes by the landlord, we should be perfectly satisfied.

The policy of the government, not only in Ottawa, but everywhere, has been not to pay taxes on buildings which we rent. Whether it is a good policy or not, I am not prepared to say. I quite understand that there are objections to it on the part of municipal authorities.

I understand that the government are exempt from taxation on any property they occupy ; but that does not prevent them carrying out the recommendation of the sub-committee of the Privy Council that in all future leases the landlord should be subject to pay taxes. We do not ask the government to pay, but we want the landlord to pay.
I would like to ask the minister if there is a sum in the estimates for the improvement of the public buildings at Brampton, Ontario ?
I am not free to speak now of the supplementary estimates, because they have not yet passed council.

I would like to ask the minister if the building which is being constructed is rented now ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, l'es, it is rented now.
Then the contract was made before the building was started ?
Yes.

Then I cannot understand why the government did not erect the building' themselves. Surely they were in as o-ood a position to erect it in time as a private individual could be. If the man who is building it is making from 18 to 20 per cent on his investment, without any taxes to pay, he is making a very good thing, and it would have been as well for the government to have made that for the country as for a private individual.
I admit that the position of the Minister of Public Works in the matter is not only an embarrassing but a ridiculous one. I quite grant that any business man would

have done what the hon. gentleman says the government should have done ; but what is my position ? I have not one dollar at my disposal. I could not expend one dollar of public money without a vote of parliament ; and, after discussion with my colleagues, they came to the conclusion that it would be better to do what we have done. The great trouble is that when there is no money voted, the Minister of Public "Works does not know what to do. He is placed at times in very embarrassing circumstances. It would have been very difficult for me to go before my colleagues and ask them to give me a Governor General's warrant for a public building. Under the circumstances it was thought best to do as we have done. But I am very glad of this criticism. Far from blaming my friends, I feel inclined to be very thankful to them. Up to the present we have been proceeding altogether on a wrong basis, and I hope that my colleagues and some of my friends will not grumble when I come before the House and ask for money to erect buildings that are necessary.

I do not think there could have been any difficulty on account of parliament not being in session, because the system of getting Governor General's warrants has been used to a very large extent in the past. I think it was used in 1896.
Not for public buildings.

It was for other matters, and it could just as well be used for public buildings as for anything else. It seems strange that the hon. gentleman's colleagues, are so lacking in business sense and perception.
I did not say so.

They must be, because it would have been a very proper thing to have saved this large amount of public money which is being expended for rent. As a new member, I had the idea that the hon. gentleman had a great deal more influence with his colleagues than he appears to have.
That is a wrong impression.
It is a matter of surprise to me to learn that the hon. gentleman is so handicapped by his colleagues. I wish it had been true in this instance that he had more influence with them.
I do not speak of myself alone. I speak of the position in which all the Ministers of Public Works have been placed. But, again, I am thankful for this debate.

have done is wrong according to hon. gentlemen opposite. The officers are clever men, and men who have been in the department for years, and I am glad to hear these statements from the other side of the House. No minister can be held responsible for these details. He must trust some-bodv, as the head of a big firm must trust the heads of branches. I cannot be responsible morally. Of course, I am responsible politically, X am fully responsible for it, and I believe my officers have done right. But I am surprised to hear so much criticism of them, considering that they are men who have such long experience, and considering the able men under whom they were trained in the past.

I do not like to find the minister seeking to shelter himself behind his officers. It is unfair to the House, and it is an unfair attack upon his officials. A few minutes ago I asked the minister who was responsible for giving Mr. Oharleson the order for these supplies, and he admitted that he wTas the man who told the officer to give Mr. Oharleson the order.
The MINISTER OF rUBLIC 'WORKS.
I never said that in my life.
I understood
No.
Did not the minister say that Mr. Ewart had to buy the supplies-
Very far from it. I said that I never knew that so much was bought of Mr. Charle-son.

The hon. minister did not know that there was $8,000 worth bought from Mr. Oharleson. But does he mean to say that he did not issue orders that these supplies were to be purchased from Mr. Charlesou ?
No, I do not believe that I ever suggested a single order to be bought from Mr. Charle-son. I may have done so. Mr. Charleson's name was placed on the patronage list, as was that of so many others.	.

What I was getting at was how the supplies were purchased from Mr. Oharleson. Will the hon. minister say that Mr. Ewart bought these goods from Mr. Charleson on his own responsibility. or was there intimation from the minister that they must be so purchased ?
The officers of the Department of Public Works have a list of those from whom they buy, I do not control these things-I do not
profess to do it, and could not do it. I do not tell my officers to buy here or there. Occasionally I say that I would like if purchases could "be made from this one or that.

Does the hon. minister mean to say that this site was selected by Mr. Ewart without it being intimated to him by the minister The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. Certainly not. I say that I acted upon the advice of my officers, and the advice of Mr. Ewart especially, he being chief architect, and a man in whom I have implicit confidence, because he is a man of competence and experience. He has been in the department for thirty years. I think it is reasonable that I should take his advice. My hon. friend (Mr. Reid, Grenville) when he hires boats must follow the advice of those who know something about it. And, in matters submitted to my charge, I follow the same course.
I admit that Mr. Ewart may have hail said that tliat building was perfectly satisfactory, but the choosing of the site and the amount paid for it, Mr. Ewart had nothing to do with.
He had everything to do with it.

The hon. minister is trying to shield himself behind his officials. There has not been a word said reflecting in the slightest degree on the officials, but simply to show that it is the minister who made the bargain for everything. I am simply trying to defend the officials in this matter. There is not one otlicial who would admit that he had anything to do with it except to carry out the .instructions of the minister, who asked him if it would do and instructed him to recommend the bargain, and the official knew very well what would happen if he did not comply. No doubt Mr. Ewart was called in and instructed to write a letter saying that the rent was a fair and just one, and if refused he would not hold his position twenty-four hours. The minister should not stand up here and try and throw any insinuations on the officials, for we believe that they are too upright and honourable to recommend this site on the annual rent except at the dictation of the hon. gentleman.

In the case of the building, the officer from the Department of the Interior suggested that site himself first as a suitable one. The matter was submitted to the chief architect, who made a report approving the site, and 1 approved the decision of the officer of the Department of the Interior and the opinion of the chief architect. I am responsible politically, and am not attempting to shirk any of that responsibility, and if my hon. friend wants to bring on a vote of con-

fidence lie is perfectly welcome to do so. I am politically responsible, but in tliis matter I took tlie advice of tlie cbief architect, a man of long experience. I am not sheltering myself behind his opinion, but have a perfect right to give that opinion in defence of the action I have taken.
Mr. REIl) (Grenville). So far as the officers are concerned, I believe they are not responsible for the site or the rent. The minister of the department generally decides these matters himself.
I did not do it myself this time, but approved of the advice given me.
The only reason I took up the matter was because the minister throws the whole blame on his officials.
No.

Yes tlie hon. gentleman is trying to shield himself behind his officials, and I thought he made a most unfair attack on men who have been in the service so many years. I know Mr.' Ewart and several of the officials, and believe they are honourable men and that although the minister has a letter signed by Mr. Ewart recommending this site and rental, if Mr. Ewart was sent on his own responsibility, he would not have chosen that site or would have given a great deal less rent for it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: J would like to ask the hon. minister if the contractors are to put in all the heating apparatus and complete the building in every particular ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: So that the building cost $15,000, and the lot $5,000.
It will come to a great deal more than that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I asked the hon. gentleman how much the building was going to cost and he did not know, and I am informed that the contract price was $12,000. The Seybold property, I am informed, was offered for sale a short time ago for $20,000, but say it is worth to-day $54,000, the government are paying 20 per cent interest on the money. In three years we will have paid $10,500 and $10,000 for permanent improvements, which makes 20 per cent interest on the money. I think it is outrageous and am going to take the sense of the House on it, and I therefore move that the item be reduced $10,000.

Well, I think it is pretty unfair, but we will, I suppose, have to stand it. What the hon. gentleman's motion means is that we must not pay the rental we have agreed to.
He may make up figures to suit himself and to prove that we are paying 20 per cent, but there is nothing easier than to put up a man of straw and then demolish him. The Seybold building is a special case, as I have explained over and over again. We had to find accommodation immediately. We required it for the 1st of April. As to the other building, it will cost in the neighbourhood of $20,000. The site cost $5,000, the contract for the bare building $17,000, the architects fee $1,000 and perhaps more, and there is an elevator costing $4,000, which makes in round numbers $27,000. Under the circumstances I do not see that I could have done anything else. I had no money to put up a building, and if I had attempted to erect a public building without a vote from parliament, there would have been twenty-five times more noise than we have now. However, I cannot help it, and let us take the sense of the House.

If the motion of my hon. friend is adopted, I doubt very much whether the course he lias pursued will commend itself even to his own judgment. The statement made by the Minister of Public Works as to the pressing necessity of providing quarters for the census bureau and enumerators, is one we ought to consider and the passage of this motion will em-barass the operations of the department in carrying on this necessary work.
Would the Minister of Public Works kindly tell us what he thinks the Seybold building is worth ?

I am not an expert in the value of land or of property. All I know is that when we want to buy property in Ottawa, we are asked pretty high prices. A few days ago I tried to buy a property, and some friend of mine told me it was worth $50,000, but I was asked $100,000 for it. It is a fact that real estate is rapidly increasing in value in the city of Ottawa. The land itself, I think is worth $40,000.
How many feet are there ?
Sixty-six feet frontage by ninety-nine.
At what is it valued for assessment purposes ?
I cannot say. I do not think you could buy the land alone to-day for $40,000. I venture to say this property is worth at least $100,000, and it is ridiculous to talk about $20000.

The government is making no use of the vacant lot.
Amendment (Mr. Taylor) to reduce the item to $21,000, negatived, and item voted.

Rideau Hall, including grounds, $17,000.

I must ask the minister to give us some idea of what this expenditure is for. I desii'e to remark here that our work would be very much shortened if we had a little more information given in the estimates. Here we have in the public accounts a volume so unwdeldly that we can scarcely carry it, giving us the audit of last year's accounts, a volume far more unwieldly than the audit of the accounts in England. But when we come to the estimates we have no information at all, and we are obliged to ask the minister all kinds of details which might very properly be given in the estimates themselves, and thus much diminish the length of the debate upon the various items. The committee will notice that where there is an increase of $25,000, or $35,000 over the preceding year, and when we are asked to vote $125,000, for instance, for ventilation, lighting, repairs, materials, furniture, &c., it is impossible for us to consent to such a vote, and do our duty to the country, without getting some information. It is regrettable that we have to press for that information, and in many instances the information is nob forthcoming as quickly as we might expect. That is the reason we have taken up so much time in discussing some of the items. I do not blame the Minister of Public Works, he complains of feeling unwell this evening, and I do not believe there is any member of the committee who would not be ready to postpone an examination of these Items if he desires it.
No.

Last evening we had under discussion the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture, and we could get very little satisfaction from him upon the larger items. The fact is that most of the information that we were calling for last night we should have had in this book, and when we applied for it to the Minister of Agriculture we had to wait for a conference between himself and his assistants upon points which, to my mind, he should have been informed upon before coming to this House. Now I take this item, it has been in the estimates nearly every year since I came to parliament. It was in the estimates before, and was very severely criticised by hon. gentlemen opposite. I am sure that there is not a member of this House who would not be pleased to vote any amount necessary to keep In a proper state of repair the residence of the Governor General, to keep it up in a way befitting the residence of the representative of the King in this country. Let me refer to the expenses of last year in connection with this object. We have, as indicated by the public accounts, at Y-3 : Rideau Hall, additional wing and furnishing, $14,128.89 ; V-S9, furniture and fix-

tures for new wing, $5,144.33 ; total indicated at V-29, $19,273.22. Then we have in the expenditure of last year's General Paylist, Rideau Hall, V-12, 121, and 122, $17,050.92 ; fuel and light, $8,000 ; remetalling drive, $1,053.86 ; a total of $45,378 last year. In the estimates for the present year we have virtually the same item reappearing, $17,000 ; for fuel and light, $8,000 ; removing snow, $2,500, or a total of $27,500. Under these circumstances I think we should know what this item- of $17,000 is. Let me say to the Minister of Public Works that I have been impressed a good deal by the temper with which he has received criticism, however heated it may have been at times, from our side of the House. Time and again the Minister of Public Works stated that he was himself happy to hear the remarks we were making, that they would give him power with his colleagues to induce them to consent to what he deemed to be the sensible thing. Therefore, although the discussion may have been prolonged, I do not think it has been lost if we have been able to impress the Minister of Public Works. For my part, though I cannot claim to be an architect or to be conversant with the management of real estate, I venture to say that I would undertake to keep the Dominion public buildings in this city in thorough repair, or at least in as good repair as they are at present, for $50,000 a year, and I could make money out of it. I am perfectly satisfied of that. I do not care what may have been spent in previous years. Nobody will make me believe that it is necessary to keep the buildings which have been indicated by the hon. Minister of Public Works in fair order to spend $125,000 a year. The moment you leave the matter of repairs in the hands of architects, you are carried far beyond what is legitimate in the way of repairs. The moment architects are called upon to make repairs, unless these repairs are of such importance that you must employ an architect, the expense is far greater. I appeal to any hon. member of this House who has had occasion to employ architects for repairs to say whether this is not so. We ought to have here a man who would not be an architect to attend to such repairs, a man of practical knowledge, a clerk of works, and I venture to say that with a system for the purchase of supplies such as they have in England and with a staff regularly employed to make these repairs, the cost of them would be reduced by more than one-lialf. I see from the statement of the hon. minister the way that these repairs are done. He knows nothing about them. Everybody who has been connected with any administration, smaller than this one, knows how difficult it is to check the mania for repairs that exists among public servants. I was for many years a member of the school board of the city of Montreal. We had eight or ten schools, and I am sure, that, mustered all

together, they were far more expensive, or at least, as expensive, as the public buildings covered by these items.
Look at the number of employees that we have to provide for.

We had ten or twelve of these schools and we had 19,000 children wearing them out. We had these repairs for $35,000 a year. We attended to that ourselves and left no discretion to the architect. We purchased supplies on the English system and we had a building committee constantly at work.
What is the English system ?

The English system is that the English government gets a list printed of everything that is required, for instance, every description of paint, nails, wood and of ail materials required. That list, which is a very complete one, is printed and the English government sends a circular to parties who have established to the satisfaction of the government that they are able to carry out their contracts, who hand in their names with that list and on that list there is one column where the British government marks down its prices for these materials and the party tendering marks his own prices, which are either more than the prices stated by the government or less, and the lowest tenderer is the party who is selected to furnish these supplies. If that system were adopted here a great deal of trouble that the hon. minister is put to would be avoided. I cannot conceive, coming from Montreal, that property should be valuable enough in any part of the city of Ottawa to command a rental of $0,500 a year. It is to me an unheard of thing and I am sure if it were known in Montreal that you could get such rentals, the people there would sell out their property and come up here. We are paying $6,500 for this property. The hon. minister might inquire how much the Cassidy Company pays for its property on that same street. We are moreover under this short rental of three years, undertaking to make improvements to the extent of $10,000. With a rental running for three years, we are making these improvements and paying $6,500 a year. It is almost $10,000, as a matter of fact, of a rental. I do not claim to know much about rentals in this city, but they are far above anything you could get for a building of that kind in Montreal.

There were years when a little less was spent and there were years when a good deal was spent at Rideau Hall. Rideau Hall is a large property, it is a pretty old property and it costs a large sum to keep it in order. Out of this $17,000, there are $9,000 spent in wages. We have a clerk
of works there. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) is suggesting that we should have a practical man. We have Mr. Hutchison who has been there for twelve or fifteen years. He has charge of ail repairs and all work at Rideau Hall. Out of this $17,000 money has to be taken to keep up the grounds, garden and so on, but, the whole work is under the direction of our architect who goes there himself many times. My hon. friend has very properly said that we must do the best we can for the Governor General and the people with him in Rideau Hall. He alluded to the expenditure of money that was incurred a -couple of years ago in erecting a new building. It was found necessary to make that addition, but it was an expenditure that will not come up again. Of the expenditure which ranges from $15,000 to $17,000, a year, $9,000 goes into wages, and the balance is employed in repairing furniture, buying new furniture and so on.
Is this work let by tender as far as possible ?
There is no tender possible. There is a staff of men who practically do what their Excellencies ask them to do in the matter of repairs.

Personally I do not like to criticise, nor would I criticise, the expenditure on behalf of the Governor General. I think the Governor General should be treated as fairly as we possibly can, but I simply rise to ask if the Governor General has control in the ordering of these supplies without doing it through the minister.
No, they make orders upon us and we authorize them. I may authorize Her Excellency to buy some little thing herself, but the accounts are always sent to us.
In this $17,000 all these items are for supplies.
No, there are $9,000 for wages and the balance is in repairs, &c.
The amount is very small for wages.

Well, admitting $9,000, the other $8,000 is for supplies. 1 think if the Governor General were allowed to spend the $8,000 himself, he could probably get a great deal more because the prices seem very much higher than what they would be if these supplies were purchased by any ordinary person. I notice here W. C. Edwards & Co., flooring $28.50. You can buy Mr. Edward's best flooring for $18 a thousand in ordinary car lots. These are exorbitant prices.

The chief architect, who ought to know something about it, and who is on the floor of the House, says we canuot buy it for less than that. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid, Grenville) is a medical man, and I suppose he knows more about it than the chief architect.
He is not practising now ; he is making money.
I apologize to him, I thought he was a medical man.

I am surprised to hear the hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid) talk as he does. He is paying about $18 a thousand for common mill-run basswood, without dressing, drawing or finishing, and he has been paying that for years for his own factory.
I am surprised to hear the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell) compare basswood with pine flooring. He knows there is as much difference between the two as between chalk and cheese.
How much difference is there ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Schell) says that I am paying $18 for common mill-run basswood, and when he says that he is making a statement which is untrue.
I do not know exactly the amount you are paying, but I know you are paying not far from $18 a thousand at Cardinal.

I am paying $19 a thousand for clear basswood, and if there is any inferior lumber it is measured out. I will ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Schell) this question : Is it not a fact that $18 a thousand is a fair price in the city of Ottawa, and that you can buy the very best pine flooring for $20 or $21 a thousand.
Is it too much to pay $28.50 for 1,297 feet ?
If it is for that quantity it is all right.
Sit down, then.
Of course everything we do is wrong, and the chief architect does not know his work.
The minister is again hiding himself behind his chief architect.
Well, if I am asked to be responsible for every piece of flooring that is bought I do not know what to say.
You are floored.
Indeed I am.

You evidently cannot take the starch out of the member for Grenville (Mr. Reid). We were astonished to learn the other day that we were to pay $3,500 a year rental for the Seybold building, but now we are told that the rent is $6,500 a year, and that in addition to that we have to pay $10,000 for alterations. For three years we pay $19,500 for rent, and $10,000 for improvements, in all $29,500, or about $10,000 a year rent to a landlord who has to pay no municipal taxes, because the buildings are rented to the Crown. Now, a lease usually carries with it the condition that if you make alterations in a rented property which are not advantageous to the property then when your lease expires you have to restore the property to the condition it was in when you rented it. I presume that to-day this building is fitted up with shelves and counters and suitable appliances for a dry goods warehouse, and if the usual clause is in the lease that we must restore the property to the condition it was in when we took possession, it may cost us some thousands of dollars more to do that. For this reason we want to see this lease, and it should be laid on the Table of the House.

The lease will be brought down ; there will be no trouble about that.
Ottawa Public Buildings-Gas and electric light, including roads and bridges, $18,500.
The same vote as last year.
That does not quite satisfy us, because last year there were very meagre explanations. I would like to have some statement as to the form of contract, and so on, with regard to this electric light.

For the first 3,000 lamps we paid $2.50 per lamp per year ; for the balance, $2 per lamp, which makes $14,500. For twenty-six arc lights on roads and bridges, at $85 each per year, we pay $2,200. We are still using gas for some purposes, for which we pay $1,200. For renewals of lamps, fittings, and so on, we pay $600, making the total of $18,500.
Is the contract for lighting so much per lamp, or do you pay by the meter ?
By the lamp.
Does that include the lighting of this building.
Yes.
Do we pay the same for a session of two months as for a session of eight months ?
We pay $2.50 per lamp for the year, which is a low price. There are many lamps that burn the whole year round, night and day, in the basements and many of the offices.
There are 960 just above us which do not burn more than one-third of the year.

These are 10-candle power ; but we pay at the rate of $2.50 for a 10-candle lamp.
Dominion Public Buildings-Salaries of engineers, firemen, caretakers, &c., $85,000.
There is an increase of $5,000.
This is for buildings all over the country, excluding Ottawa. The increase is because we have more public buildings in all parts of Canada, Nova Scotia included.

I may have to criticise the hon. gentleman, because we are very anxious to see public buildings there. In the city of Halifax we have been waiting for three years. I hope my hon. friend is not charging us with rent before we have the building.
The chief architect tells me that the plans for that building are nearly completed, and my hon. friend will have the pleasure of having one of the finest buildings in Canada.

Before we leave /this item, I should like to point out that the hon. gentleman is getting $224,000 for the maintenance, heating, and lighting of the public buildings in Ottawa, exclusive of Rideau Hall and the experimental farm-just for the departmental buildings. I should be inclined to think that with that very moderate sum at his command, he should be able to keep them in reasonably good order during the ensuing year.

It is a problem. I will do my best. Whether it is myself or somebody else, there is not much pleasure in it.
Harbours and Rivers, N.S.-Abbott's Harbour -Beach protection works, $1,105.
Is this an additional work ?

It is an additional work, and this will complete it.
Beaver River, N.S.-Extension wharf, $2,100.

That will complete the work.
Big Bras d'Or-Wharf-Repairs, $400.

That will complete the work.
Boularderie Centre-Wharf, $1,100.

That will complete the work.
Canada Creek Breakwater-New block, $500.
What is the new block?

It is found necessary to build a kind of block at the end of the wharf.
Cape Negro Island-Repairs to and extension of breakwater, $500.

This will complete the work.
Chebogue-Harbour protection work, $1,320.

This will complete the work.
Cheverie-Breakwater extension, $4,000.
What is the purpose of this breakwater ?
It is an extension of the old work, 100 feet in length and 20 feet wide. The existing breakwater was 130 feet long, and we are adding that length to give additional protection.
Are all these works done under contract ?
This work is done by day's labour. Some of the others were done under contract, and many of them by day's labour.
Why were not all done under contract ?

Because that is not always practicable. The repairs cannot easily be done by contract, and when you can find a good foreman it is much better and cheaper to have the work done by day's labour. Of course, I generally advertise all our important works.
The hon. gentleman says it is better in many instances to do the work by day's labour. No one would expect him to be precise and say it was better in the interests of the party.

It is better in the public interest. It gives more trouble, and the minister has no possible interest in having the work done by day labour, but workmen have their rights and prefer day labour. The contractors have to make profit out of the men, and I do not see why the government should not be their own contractors. I am speaking as one who has acquired a pretty valuable experience in the conduct of these works, and I have found that whenever you

can find a good foreman, work done by day labour is preferable to contract work. But nevertheless, most of our works are advertised, as my hon. friend knows.
The legitimate conclusion from the hon. gentleman's statement is that, under all circumstances when you can get a good foreman, it is better to have the work by day's labour than by contract.
I did not say that.

It would be very difficult to draw any other conclusion from the hon. gentleman's statement. The experience of the whole world is quite at variance with his. There is no business man in Ottawa, who, if he had a block of buildings to erect, would think for a moment of employing a foreman and having it erected by day labour. Men who are working for the government feel that they have more latitude than they would if working for contractors, and do about just as they please. No ten men in Ottawa will do as much work by day labour on a public building as they would for a contractor. In some cases, it is no doubt impossible to do the work otherwise than by day labour, but the cardinal rule should be that wherever possible the contract system should be adopted. Otherwise, only men are engaged by the day who are in political accord with the party in power. Why, my hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) has told how in his own city, if a man was not of one political stripe, he could not be employed on the building being constructed with public money. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) may not know of this particular case, but he has a general knowledge of what goes on all over the country, and he cannot be absolved from the responsibility. I hope he will retract his statement, and that he will enter upon the sound and wholesome course of having work done wherever possible under contract. I recognize that much of the work of the hon. gentleman's department and of other departments ns well, must be done by day's labour. But. we should have a reiteration of the sound principle, at one time advocated by the Liberal party, of public tender and contract. I see hon. gentlemen on the other side who did the country groat service by advocating this principle. I recognize the good they did. though it led them to criticise the party with which I am in sympathy. But I would ask these hon. gentlemen to take the same course to-day and not to accept silently the declaration of the hon. Minister of Public Works that work should be done by day's labour, and not by contract. If we do not have a retraction of the hon. minister's statement, but if that is to indicate our course for the future, we may well despair of any fair return for the people's money expended in public works.

My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is not, I am sorry to see, a progressive man. There are some progressive countries, New Zealand, for instance, that have done away with the system of advertising for contracts.
That does not prove the system wrong.

No, but it proves that in some enlightened countries, and British colonies, the workmen have learned to assert themselves, and public men have learned to appreciate the position of the workers. I say, as I have often said before, that I am in favour of day's labour wherever the circumstances will allow it. I have never hidden my views. It is true that I have not always followed my own views, for most of the works carried on in my departments have been advertised. But I say without hesitation that workmen are better treated and they do as much work for us as they do for a contractor-
No.

Yes, they do as much work-provided you secure a good foreman ; that is the essential condition. The hon. gentleman has not enough confidence in the workingmen of his country. I say that the workingmen are just as houourable as any other class. Treat them well and they will give you good work. That is the reason why I say without any hesitation whatever that work carried out by workmen under proper supervision is a system that should not be denounced by any man who follows the progress of the country. This is not the first time I have stood in this House and advocated the system of day's labour. Again, I say I have not always followed my own view. I fear I have not followed them often enough. I should have been given more latitude. Suppose the Department of Public Works and the Department of Railways should train a certain number of foremen and that we should do our work ourselves. There is no reason why we should not succeed. The workingmen would be better treated and the contractors would not make the profits out of their earnings. For very large works, perhaps, we are not prepared now for this system ; but the day is not very far distant when my hon. friend will not dare to express the views he has expressed to-day. For the workingmen are asserting themselves. I am not a demagogue, far from it. But I say that the workingmen of this country are growing better educated every day, and they are entitled to fair treatment at the hands of the government. I rebuilt the Western Block by day's labour, and I challenge any man to show that there was $25 of useless expenditure. The work has been splendidly done by union men. We are not ready yet to carry out that system

as I would like to do. In tills country we have stood by tbe system of the lowest tenderer. I state without hesitation, after five years of experience, that the system of the lowest tenderer as it is practiced here is an infernally bad one. If it were practiced as it is praticed in England, Germany or France, it would be a good system. In those countries they ask tenders from a selected list of competent men. But we ask publicly for tenders. Any Tom, Dick or Harry may put in a tender. Sometimes you get a tender which your chief engineer or architect reports far too low. But the man who makes the tender is able to put up a deposit, and you are morally bound to give him the work. The consequence is that he does not pay his men, that he does not pay for his materials. I admit that since I became Minister of Public Works I have had dozens and dozens of cases like that.
It was the hon. gentleman's own fault.

Of course, I am guilty of everything. As to the case in St. Thomas, an hon. gentleman who is an old member of the House, has told us that in order for a man to secure work on a public building there, he must be a Liberal. But what are the facts : I have' stated them before, but I will state them again, for I cannot allow the hon. gentleman's statement to pass unchallenged. The contract for the work in St. Thomas was given to the lowest tenderer. Can I interfere there, can I say to that contractor: You must hire this man, or you must discharge that one ? But I fear we have departed from the item under debate.
The hon. gentleman in his earnestness has not yet told us what the original purpose of this breakwater was.
It was to give protection to ships.
To form a harbour ?
Yes.

I do not propose to allow the hon. Minister of Public Works to give a free lecture such as he has given, without an answer. The hon. gentleman declares that he is not a demagogue. But I venture to tell the hon. gentleman that he is, unconsciously perhaps, one of the greatest demagogues the country ever new. Now the hon. gentleman declares that it is in the interest of the workingmen. I tell him that the moment he assumes the parental care of the workingmen of this country they have a very doubtful sponsor. What does that mean in the hands of a minister of this country ? Why, it means that these political hacks will get all the work, and that none
others will; it means that the workingmen are all selected by the hon. gentleman himself or by his minions. There is not a little twopenny-hapenny public work going in Canada to-day in which you cannot trace the hand of the Minister of Public Works. The hon. gentleman is very indignant about that case in the city of St. Thomas. When my hon. friend from Elgin (Mr. Ingram) declared that the work was only given to Liberals, the minister asked, What difference 'does that make ? Does he not know that a contractor's life would not be worth anything as a contractor if he did not give the work to Liberals ? If he did not agree to the exactions made upon him by the men put over him by the minister, his contract would be utterly worthless. I know some most disgraceful cases. The hon. gentleman sent a dredge up to the River Sydenham. His agent, before he knew the political complexion of the parties, went unwittingly and bought a little butcher's meat on several occasions while the dredge was working there. This man was told one day that it had been discovered that he was a Conservative, and he could no longer furnish a few pounds of fresh meat to the dredge. I venture to say that is going on from one end of Canada to the other. It seems a very dangerous thing to allow a minister of the Crown to control so much patronage when he permits a thing of that kind.	[DOT]

Not only did I not permit it, but I had no knowledge of that case. The hon. gentleman has been misinformed. How could I interfere with that man ? Suppose he does not want to give the work to friends of hon, gentlemen opposite, what have I got to do with that ? That man is free.

No man is free under the hon. gentleman. The moment a man comes under the power of his department, he is a slave afterwards. When the hon. gentleman parades himself as the champion of the workingmen and takes the public money and gives it to his heelers, then I tell him he is a menace to the workingmen of this country, and a menace to their interests. Men who are not in political accord with the hon. gentleman might just as well go to the poor house as look for work from him. The workingmen of this country understand him very well.

Since I have been on this side of the House I admit that I have given patronage to our political friends. Hon. gentlemen opposite did the same thing for their friends during 20 years. They seem now to have forgotten that. What is the use of singing that tune here ? We all know that patronage belongs to the party in office. At present, other things being equal, the patronage belongs to the Liberal party. We have been out of office for eighteen years, now we have

been In office only four or five years, and yet bon. gentlemen opposite already grumble and cry as if they had been out of office for eighteen years. When they have been eighteen years out of office they will have some right to complain. But after they have only been five years out of office, they already begin to complain. Really they should take their medicine with better grace. Now, it may be that in the riding of my hon. friend, the man in charge of the dredge was instructed to buy meat from the political friends' of the party in power. That was the proper thing to do. When lion, gentlemen opposite get over to this side of the House again, they will do the same thing, they know it perfectly well. They will do what we are doing. But there is one thing in which they will not imitate us. We have left too much in the hands of employees appointed by bon. gentlemen opposite. This government has suffered more criticism at the hands of its friends than our hon. friends opposite seem to know. Ministers of the Crown have been assailed by our friends on this side, and reproached violently because we have not dismissed enough men, because we have not given all the patronage to our friends.
I do not think you are to blame.

I do not deny that I have done my best to serve the Liberal party, and I believe I have not committed an injustice willingly, anyhow. I do not believe I have dismissed a man unfairly, I do not believe I have wasted public money. Other things equal, I have favoured the Liberal party, as it was right to do, and I may add, as it was my duty to do.

The minister says that because my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) is opposed to certain works being done by contract, that therefore my hon. friend is opposed to the interests of the workingmen. Am I correct in sizing up the hon, gentleman's argument ? Will the hon. gentleman answer ?
Let the hon. gentleman go on, we are not in confession here.

I am sure if the hon. gentleman made a confession he would find himself in an embarrassing position. I remember some years ago. when the Conservative government were making repairs to certain harbours and were doing them by day labour, no hon. gentleman in this House took a stronger stand against the government at that time than did the present Minister of Public Works. I maintain that it is impossible in many cases to ask for tenders for the improvement of harbours. I believe that owing to the fact of a public work being in a state of decay, to piers Mr. TARTE.
being in a dilapidated state, it is often impossible for either a government engineer or any other person to ask for tenders to complete the improvement of a harbour. That is a case, in my mind, that cannot be done by contract, but there are cases, and in my county at the present time there is a work going on that could have been let by contract if the government desired to let it by contract. I do not say that the government would derive any advantage by letting it by contract.
What work is that ?

That is the improvement of the Port Burwell harbour. The improvement of the Port Stanley harbour is being done by day's work and I want to say to the hon. minister that there has not been a Conservative employed on that harbour, and there will not be a Conservative employed there, so long as the gentleman who has the patronage of that riding has the patronage of this government. I may say that Port Burwell is not subject to the whim of the gentleman who has the patronage of East Elgin, and the work is being done in a creditable manner by the gentleman who has charge of it.
Hear, hear.

In respect to the purchase of supplies from the friends of the government, I quite admit that, all things being equal, the friends of the government have a right to furnish supplies. But, while I admit, that, all things being equal, the government have a perfect right to give this patronage to their friends, if they are not equal, then, the furnishing of these supplies should not be given to their personal or political friends.
I quite agree that that is a sound principle.
Has that principle been violated ?
It has not been violated.
I think the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) has not very far to seek for a violation of that principle.
I do not know of its having been violated there.

I am afraid my hon. friend would be very hard to convince that a violation lias occurred. I am afraid that he is as blind as the Minister of Public Works. In respect to the armoury at St. Thomas, I am sorry to say that the patronage is not always controlled by a man, but that the other side of the House appears to have something to do with the patronage in East Elgin." I do know that the word has gone forth that no Conservative can lay any bricks on the armoury.
31G1
I never heard a word of that.
I would like to know if the lion. Minister of Public Works is aware of that.
I am not aware of it. This is the first intimation that I have got of such a state of affairs, and I have never given any orders of that kind.
Will the hon. gentleman remedy any case if he finds the statement to be correct ?

I would like to ask lion, gentlemen opposite what they would do if they were only here. Here is a contractor who was the lowest tenderer. Have I a right to tell him: You must not employ this man, or that man ?
The hon. gentleman has a right to lay down a rule.
I cannot interfere. The only thing I can do is to see that he has delivered the goods he has undertaken to deliver to me.

Would the hon. gentleman say, to be perfectly fair in a discussion of this kind, if a vicious principle were admitted upon both sides of the House to obtain throughout the country, that he could not prevent that or that he could not take precautions in the letting of his contracts guarding against a recurrence of it ?
Certainly not.
